metadata.summary: This guideline addresses diagnosis, management and follow-up of common vulval inflammatory conditions, vulvodynia and vulval intraepithelial neoplasia. It covers investigations, topical and systemic treatments, procedures, supportive measures and considerations during pregnancy and breast-feeding. It also describes multidisciplinary care and referral between relevant clinical specialties.

conditions_covered: Primary or idiopathic lichen simplex chronicus
Low-grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (SIL) of the vulva or vulval LSIL
High-grade SIL of the vulva or vulval HSIL

toxicities.event: Stinging or local irritation after topical application
recognition: Stinging or irritation at the application site.

toxicities.event: Contact allergy to a topical preparation
recognition: A treatment that previously worked becomes less effective.

management.actions: Consider allergy testing. For suspected vulval allergic contact dermatitis, testing should include medicaments, preservatives and products the patient applies to the vulva, alongside the standard baseline allergens.

prevention: Prefer ointment bases on anogenital skin because they generally require fewer preservatives than creams.

toxicities.event: Contact dermatitis or local infection reported during treatment of vulval psoriasis
Skin atrophy associated with topical steroid exposure
prevention: For children with lichen sclerosus, the regimen of daily application for one month, application on alternate days for one month and twice-weekly application for one month may be preferred to avoid skin atrophy.
Limit each application to a maximum of 15 min.
Avoid retinoids during pregnancy and for at least 2 years before conception; use caution in females of child-bearing age.
After retinoid treatment for lichen sclerosus or acitretin treatment for hypertrophic lichen planus, avoid pregnancy for at least 2 years.
The documented occurrence of carcinomas after PUVA and UVB warrants particular concern when considering treatment at the genital site.

recognition: Eruptions resembling LP, including erosive oral and vulval disease.
prevention: Reserve these drugs for only the most recalcitrant vulval lichen planus cases.

toxicities.event: Recurrence of lichen sclerosus around a surgical scar
recognition: Reappearance of disease around the scar.
prevention: Limit surgery to coexistent VIN/SCC or fusion. For clitoral fusion, operate only in rare situations, using an experienced surgeon after counselling about adverse effects and possible recurrence.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Vaccination was introduced to reduce cervical premalignant and malignant lesions and other HPV-related lesions, including HSIL. The guideline reports prevention of HPV 16- and 18-related high-grade vulval and vaginal lesions with the quadrivalent HPV 6/11/16/18 and bivalent (16/18) vaccines in women negative for HPV 16 or 18 before vaccination; it reports slightly better prevention with the nonavalent vaccine (HPV 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58). It does not specify a vaccination schedule.

For genital lichen sclerosus, twice-weekly maintenance with, for example, mometasone furoate 0.1% ointment or clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment maintains remission and may help prevent malignant change. Treat asymptomatic disease to prevent scarring.
After surgical adhesiolysis for vulvo–vaginal LP, routinely apply potent topical steroids immediately; the guideline reports improved long-term outcomes and function.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients undergoing surgical adhesiolysis for vulvo–vaginal LP.

infection_management.management: Consider screening in all patients according to symptoms and risk factors. Investigate for concurrent infections when lesions do not heal with standard treatment. Partner tracing is required only if screening identifies a sexually transmitted infection.
Test for both when genital ulcers are present, including when an ulcerating dermatosis is also present.
Consider testing in all patients, particularly those with atypical common skin disorders, numerous hyperkeratotic warts, treatment-resistant seborrheic dermatitis, or new or severe psoriasis.

Exclude candidiasis when vulval itch is accompanied particularly by increased discharge. If symptoms persist after anti-candidal treatment, especially with negative candida cultures, perform a full genital examination including speculum examination unless recently performed, and consider other causes.
Use appropriate swabs when evaluating vulval dermatitis. Treat coexisting infection with a steroid/antifungal or steroid/antibacterial combination.

If secondary infection is a concern, a potent or ultra-potent topical steroid combined with antibacterial and antifungal agents, or another preparation that addresses the infection, may be appropriate. Use it only briefly to clear the infection. Obtain bacterial, fungal or viral swabs only when symptoms or signs suggest coexisting infection.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Secondary infection in vulval lichen planus
infection_management.management: Take a skin swab to exclude secondary infection, particularly in excoriated lesions.
Consider it in the differential diagnosis of a well-defined annular or circinate erythema with a papular or pustular edge and peripheral scaling; skin scrapings can help exclude it.
Consider primary infection or superinfection when assessing symmetrical vulval erythema.

therapies_index.name: Simple emollients
approved_indications: General vulval care as a soap substitute and moisturizer
therapies_index.administration: Apply to the vulval skin; a barrier emollient may be applied regularly to affected areas.

therapies_index.name: emulsifying ointment
approved_indications: Soap substitute for vulval dermatitis
Vulval care in vulvodynia
therapies_index.administration: Use as a soap substitute.

therapies_index.name: Barrier preparations
therapies_index.mechanism: Provide a protective barrier against local irritants.
approved_indications: Vulval dermatitis when urinary incontinence is substantial
therapies_index.administration: Apply to affected areas.

therapies_index.name: hydrocortisone
approved_indications: Mild vulval dermatitis
therapies_index.administration: Use 1% hydrocortisone ointment once daily for 7–10 days until symptoms and signs resolve, then as needed for recurrence.

therapies_index.name: mometasone furoate
approved_indications: More severe vulval dermatitis
Milder lichen simplex chronicus
Genital lichen sclerosus and maintenance of its remission
therapies_index.administration: For vulval dermatitis, apply once daily for 7–10 days, then as needed. For milder lichen simplex chronicus, use mometasone furoate 0.1% ointment once or twice daily and taper when improvement occurs. For maintenance of lichen sclerosus remission, mometasone furoate 0.1% ointment may be applied twice weekly.
monitoring: Review lichen sclerosus treatment response after 3 months.

therapies_index.name: betamethasone valerate
approved_indications: More severe vulval dermatitis
therapies_index.administration: Apply betamethasone valerate 0.025% once daily for 7–10 days until symptoms and signs resolve, then as needed for recurrence.

therapies_index.name: Antihistamines
approved_indications: Sleep disturbance associated with vulval dermatitis

therapies_index.name: tacrolimus
approved_indications: Unlicensed option for resistant vulval dermatitis
Unlicensed treatment reported effective for vulval psoriasis
Unlicensed second-line treatment for lichen simplex chronicus
Unlicensed treatment studied for lichen sclerosus
Alternative topical treatment that may be effective for vulval lichen planus
therapies_index.administration: For lichen simplex chronicus, tacrolimus 0.1% ointment twice daily for up to 12 weeks. Studies in lichen sclerosus used topical tacrolimus 0.1% daily for 12 weeks or for 16 to 24 weeks; topical tacrolimus 0.03% ointment was described for children and twice-weekly maintenance.
key_toxicities: Stinging on application in resistant vulval dermatitis
Contact dermatitis and local mycotic or viral infections reported with topical calcineurin inhibitors for vulval psoriasis
Local irritation reported during initial use in lichen sclerosus
monitoring: Long-term risks in lichen sclerosus require further study because of concern about malignancy with topical immunosuppression.

therapies_index.name: pimecrolimus
approved_indications: Unlicensed option for resistant vulval dermatitis
Unlicensed treatment reported effective for vulval psoriasis
Unlicensed second-line treatment for lichen simplex chronicus
Unlicensed treatment studied for lichen sclerosus
Alternative topical treatment that may be effective for vulval lichen planus
therapies_index.administration: For lichen simplex chronicus, pimecrolimus 1% cream twice daily for up to 12 weeks. Studies in vulval lichen sclerosus assessed pimecrolimus 1% cream after 12 weeks and after 6 months application.
key_toxicities: Stinging on application in resistant vulval dermatitis
Contact dermatitis and local mycotic or viral infections reported with topical calcineurin inhibitors for vulval psoriasis
Local irritation reported during initial use in lichen sclerosus
monitoring: Long-term risks in lichen sclerosus require further study because of concern about malignancy with topical immunosuppression.

therapies_index.name: Topical corticosteroids
approved_indications: Localized vulval psoriasis
Vulval dermatitis
Lichen simplex chronicus
Genital lichen sclerosus
Vulval lichen planus
therapies_index.administration: For vulval psoriasis, use mid potency topical steroids followed by low potency topical steroids in sequential or rotational regimens; frequency and duration depend on the agent and response. For genital lichen sclerosus, commonly apply a potent to ultra-potent preparation once daily for three months, or daily for one month, on alternate days for one month and twice weekly for one month; twice-daily application may occasionally help resistant disease.
key_toxicities: Skin atrophy is a consideration with treatment in children with lichen sclerosus.
monitoring: Review lichen sclerosus response at 3 months.
Review vulval dermatitis when a more potent topical steroid is needed.
Review severe lichen simplex chronicus treated with potent topical corticosteroids after 4 weeks.

therapies_index.name: Topical vitamin D analogues
approved_indications: Localized vulval psoriasis, alone or with topical corticosteroids
therapies_index.administration: Apply topically, either alone or with topical corticosteroids; no specific schedule is given.

therapies_index.name: Coal tar preparations
approved_indications: Suggested topical option for vulval psoriasis, alone or with topical corticosteroids
therapies_index.administration: One example is 1–5% liquor carbonis detergens in aqueous cream. Short periods of topical use during pregnancy are considered to pose only a small risk.

therapies_index.name: Crisaborole
therapies_index.mechanism: Described as a non-steroidal topical agent.
approved_indications: Atopic dermatitis; a 2020 study reported promising results in genital psoriasis
therapies_index.administration: Topical; no schedule is given.

therapies_index.name: Dapsone
approved_indications: Reported effective in vulval pustular psoriasis with topical treatment
Empirically tried for vulvo–vaginal–gingival syndrome, with general agreement that it provides little or no benefit
therapies_index.administration: For vulval pustular psoriasis, 100 mg/day for 1 month alongside topical treatment.

therapies_index.name: methotrexate
approved_indications: Systemic option for disseminated or generalized psoriasis with genital involvement or genital psoriasis refractory to topical regimens
Systemic option with limited evidence for vulval erosive lichen planus
therapies_index.administration: Standard doses are mentioned for lichen planus, without a specified regimen.
monitoring: Potentially toxic systemic treatment for lichen planus requiring careful monitoring, preferably under a dermatologist in a specialized clinic.

therapies_index.name: retinoids
approved_indications: Systemic option for disseminated or generalized psoriasis with genital involvement or genital psoriasis refractory to topical regimens
Possible option for genital lichen sclerosus after standard therapy fails
therapies_index.administration: For lichen sclerosus, treatment should be provided only by a dermatologist experienced with these agents.
key_toxicities: Severe teratogenicity; pregnancy must be avoided for at least 2 years after treatment for lichen sclerosus.

therapies_index.name: cyclosporine
approved_indications: Systemic option for disseminated or generalized psoriasis with genital involvement or genital psoriasis refractory to topical regimens
Possible systemic option for selected cases of vulval lichen planus
monitoring: Potentially toxic systemic treatment for lichen planus requiring careful monitoring, preferably under a dermatologist in a specialized clinic.

therapies_index.name: Ixekizumab
approved_indications: Genital psoriasis; a phase 3 trial reported improvement in genital erosions, ulcers, fissures, pruritus and sexual life

therapies_index.name: Secukinumab
approved_indications: Genital psoriasis; a 2021 study reported efficacy and safety similar to ixekizumab

therapies_index.name: Ustekinumab
approved_indications: Genital psoriasis

therapies_index.name: Guselkumab
approved_indications: Genital and facial psoriasis; an observational study reported favourable results

therapies_index.name: anthralin
key_toxicities: Possible local adverse reactions, mainly irritation, when used for vulval psoriasis.

therapies_index.name: tazarotene
key_toxicities: Possible local adverse reactions, mainly irritation, when used for vulval psoriasis.

therapies_index.name: saline soaks
approved_indications: Improvement of skin barrier function in lichen simplex chronicus
therapies_index.administration: Use before lubricants, which subsequently replace the soaks.

therapies_index.name: Petroleum-based lubricants
key_toxicities: Described as excessively greasy and not recommended for lichen simplex chronicus.

therapies_index.name: clobetasol propionate
approved_indications: Severe lichen simplex chronicus
First-line treatment and remission maintenance for genital lichen sclerosus
First-line topical treatment for vulval erosive lichen planus
therapies_index.administration: For severe lichen simplex chronicus, clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment once or twice daily, tapered slowly as improvement occurs. For lichen sclerosus maintenance, clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment twice weekly; thirty grams of an ultra-potent steroid should last at least 3 months. No optimal schedule is established for vulval erosive lichen planus.
monitoring: Review severe lichen simplex chronicus after 4 weeks.
Assess lichen sclerosus response after 3 months.

therapies_index.name: fluticasone propionate
approved_indications: Milder lichen simplex chronicus
therapies_index.administration: Apply fluticasone propionate 0.005% once or twice daily and taper after improvement.

therapies_index.name: triamcinolone
approved_indications: Very thick lichen simplex chronicus plaques
therapies_index.administration: Intralesional injection.

therapies_index.name: Intermittent ice application
approved_indications: Symptom relief in lichen simplex chronicus
therapies_index.administration: Apply intermittently for a maximum of 15 min.
key_toxicities: Cold injury if application exceeds the advised maximum.

therapies_index.name: hydroxyzine
approved_indications: Night-time scratching in lichen simplex chronicus
therapies_index.administration: Used as a sedative antihistamine; no dose is given.

therapies_index.name: amitriptyline
approved_indications: Night-time scratching in lichen simplex chronicus
Frequently used for vulvodynia, although evidence is insufficient to support benefit and two small RCT studies did not confirm efficacy
therapies_index.administration: For vulvodynia, usually 5 to 50 mg daily; no dose is given for lichen simplex chronicus.
key_toxicities: Tolerance is frequently poor in vulvodynia treatment.

therapies_index.name: Narrow band ultraviolet B
approved_indications: Alternative treatment for lichen simplex chronicus
therapies_index.administration: Delivered with a comb-like instrument.

therapies_index.name: Excimer 308-nm laser
therapies_index.mechanism: Its effect in lichen simplex chronicus may involve reduced cellular DNA damage and epidermal hyperinnervation.
approved_indications: Alternative treatment for lichen simplex chronicus

therapies_index.name: High-intensity focused ultrasound
approved_indications: Alternative treatment for lichen simplex chronicus

therapies_index.name: Silk fabric underwear
approved_indications: Possible reduction in topical steroid use for lichen simplex chronicus
therapies_index.administration: Wear as underwear.

therapies_index.name: gentamycin
approved_indications: Example of an antibacterial agent combined with a topical steroid and antifungal when secondary infection complicates lichen sclerosus
therapies_index.administration: Use the combination only briefly to clear infection.

therapies_index.name: fucidic acid
approved_indications: Example of an antibacterial agent combined with a topical steroid and antifungal when secondary infection complicates lichen sclerosus
therapies_index.administration: Use the combination only briefly to clear infection.

therapies_index.name: nystatin
approved_indications: Example of an antifungal agent combined with a topical steroid and antibacterial when secondary infection complicates lichen sclerosus
therapies_index.administration: Use the combination only briefly to clear infection.

therapies_index.name: azole antifungals
approved_indications: Antifungal option combined with a topical steroid and antibacterial when secondary infection complicates lichen sclerosus
therapies_index.administration: Use the combination only briefly to clear infection.

therapies_index.name: aciretin
approved_indications: Example of a systemic retinoid that may be considered after standard treatment for genital lichen sclerosus fails
therapies_index.administration: Only a dermatologist experienced with retinoids should prescribe treatment.
key_toxicities: Severe teratogenicity; pregnancy must be avoided for at least 2 years after finishing treatment.

therapies_index.name: acitretin
approved_indications: May help hypertrophic vulval lichen planus
therapies_index.administration: Pregnancy must be avoided for 2 years after finishing treatment.
key_toxicities: Severe teratogenicity; absolutely contraindicated during pregnancy.
monitoring: Potentially toxic systemic treatment for lichen planus requiring careful monitoring, preferably under a dermatologist in a specialized clinic.

therapies_index.name: UVA1 phototherapy
approved_indications: May be considered for lichen sclerosus when topical corticosteroids fail
Potential first-line option for extragenital lichen sclerosus

therapies_index.name: PUVA
key_toxicities: Documented development of carcinomas raises concern about use for lichen sclerosus, particularly at genital sites.

therapies_index.name: UVB
key_toxicities: Documented development of carcinomas raises concern about use for lichen sclerosus, particularly at genital sites.

therapies_index.name: laser
approved_indications: Studied for lichen sclerosus, but a systematic review found no high-quality supporting evidence
key_toxicities: Long-term adverse-effect data for treatment of lichen sclerosus are lacking.

therapies_index.name: Surgery
approved_indications: For lichen sclerosus, limited to coexisting VIN/SCC or fusion
For lichen planus, may be necessary for symptomatic vulval or vaginal adhesions and scarring
therapies_index.administration: Surgery for clitoral fusion in lichen sclerosus is reserved for rare situations, performed by an experienced surgeon after counselling. Surgery for lichen planus is contraindicated during active inflammatory disease.
key_toxicities: Lichen sclerosus may recur around the surgical scar in females.
Clitoral fusion can recur after surgery.
Sexual difficulties may persist after surgery for lichen planus.

therapies_index.name: calcipotriol
approved_indications: May be tried for extragenital lichen sclerosus
therapies_index.administration: Apply topically, possibly under occlusion.

therapies_index.name: hydrocortisone rectal foam
approved_indications: Possible vaginal corticosteroid delivery for lichen planus
therapies_index.administration: Introduce into the vagina with an applicator 1–2 times daily.

therapies_index.name: Prednisolone suppositories
approved_indications: More severe vaginal lichen planus
therapies_index.administration: Use as vaginal suppositories; no schedule is given.

therapies_index.name: hydroxychloroquine
approved_indications: Systemic option with limited evidence for vulval lichen planus
therapies_index.administration: Standard doses are mentioned, without a specified regimen.
monitoring: Potentially toxic systemic treatment for lichen planus requiring careful monitoring, preferably under a dermatologist in a specialized clinic.

therapies_index.name: mycophenolate mofetil
approved_indications: Systemic option worth considering for selected vulval lichen planus cases
therapies_index.administration: Standard doses are mentioned, without a specified regimen.
monitoring: Potentially toxic systemic treatment for lichen planus requiring careful monitoring, preferably under a dermatologist in a specialized clinic.

therapies_index.name: prednisolone
approved_indications: Severe flares of vulval lichen planus
therapies_index.administration: An example is oral prednisolone 40 mg/day, tapered over a few weeks; courses may be repeated if needed.
monitoring: Potentially toxic systemic treatment for lichen planus requiring careful monitoring, preferably under a dermatologist in a specialized clinic.

therapies_index.name: TNF-a inhibitors
approved_indications: Reserved for only the most recalcitrant lichen planus cases
key_toxicities: Reported to induce LP-like eruptions, including erosive oral and vulval disease.
monitoring: Potentially toxic systemic treatment for lichen planus requiring careful monitoring, preferably under a dermatologist in a specialized clinic.

therapies_index.name: basiliximab
approved_indications: A single case report described effectiveness in severe erosive oral LP; use in vulval disease has not been evaluated

therapies_index.name: surgical lysis of vulvo–vaginal adhesions
approved_indications: Symptomatic vulval and vaginal adhesions or scarring in lichen planus when inflammatory disease is not active
therapies_index.administration: Potent topical steroids should be used routinely immediately after adhesiolysis.
key_toxicities: Sexual difficulties may persist after surgery.

therapies_index.name: focused ultrasound therapy
approved_indications: A prospective study reported responses in non-neoplastic epithelial vulval disorders, including vulval LP

therapies_index.name: lidocaine
approved_indications: Mainly prescribed for introital dyspareunia associated with provoked vestibulodynia; long-term daily use was not more effective than placebo for vestibular pain
therapies_index.administration: Apply 5% lidocaine ointment or 2% lidocaine gel 10–20 min before penetrative sex and wash off immediately before penetration. The ineffective long-term regimen studied used Lidocaine 5% four times a day for 12 weeks.

therapies_index.name: Botulinum neurotoxin
approved_indications: Studied for vulvodynia; injection was not superior to placebo for pain reduction
therapies_index.administration: Inject 20–50 units into the bulbo-cavernosus muscles.

therapies_index.name: amitryptiline
approved_indications: 2% topical cream was investigated for vulvodynia, alone or with baclofen; efficacy remains to be established
therapies_index.administration: 2% cream applied topically; no schedule is given.

therapies_index.name: baclofen
approved_indications: Investigated with 2% amitryptiline cream for vulvodynia; efficacy remains to be established
therapies_index.administration: Used with topical 2% amitryptiline cream; no dose or schedule is given.

therapies_index.name: capsaicin
approved_indications: Investigated for vulvodynia; benefit has not been demonstrated
therapies_index.administration: 0.025% to 0.05% capsaicin cream; no schedule is given.
key_toxicities: Burning limits use.

therapies_index.name: Cannabis
approved_indications: Insufficient evidence to recommend it for vulvodynia

therapies_index.name: Desimipramine
approved_indications: Studied for vulvodynia; it was not superior to placebo
therapies_index.administration: Increase dosage from 25 mg to 150 mg over 12 weeks.

therapies_index.name: milnacipran
approved_indications: A study reported reduced coital pain in vulvodynia
therapies_index.administration: Oral milnacipran, 50–200 mg per day for 12 weeks.

therapies_index.name: Gabapentin
approved_indications: Studied for vulvodynia; it was not more effective than placebo for tampon test pain or dyspareunia, although a positive effect on sexual function was reported
therapies_index.administration: 1200 to 3000 mg per day.

therapies_index.name: pregabalin
approved_indications: Investigated for vulvodynia, with little supporting evidence

therapies_index.name: Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve stimulation (TENS)
approved_indications: Vulvodynia, preferably as part of a multidimensional approach
therapies_index.administration: May be self-administered.

therapies_index.name: fractional CO 2 laser therapy
approved_indications: Studied for vulvodynia; efficacy has not been established

therapies_index.name: low-level laser therapy
approved_indications: Studied for vulvodynia; efficacy has not been established

therapies_index.name: radiofrequency
approved_indications: Studied for vulvodynia; efficacy has not been established

therapies_index.name: Acupuncture
approved_indications: Vulvodynia; small clinical trials reported benefits for pain and sexual functioning, alone or alongside lidocaine
therapies_index.administration: Alone or with lidocaine; no schedule is given.

therapies_index.name: Physical therapy
therapies_index.mechanism: Targets pelvic floor proprioception, relaxation, discrimination, elasticity and muscle tone, as well as desensitization of painful vulval tissue.
approved_indications: First-line treatment for vulvodynia
therapies_index.administration: Includes education, pelvic floor exercises with biofeedback, manual therapy and dilation, separately or together; the best results are described with physiotherapists experienced in chronic vulval pain and its sexual effects.

therapies_index.name: Psychosexual interventions
therapies_index.mechanism: Address thoughts, emotions, behaviours and couple interactions associated with vulvodynia.
approved_indications: Vulvodynia, including its effects on pain, sexual function, sexual well-being and relationships
therapies_index.administration: May include cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT), pain management, sex therapy and psychoeducation, offered alone or together.

therapies_index.name: Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT)
approved_indications: Vulvodynia; a comparison reported greater reduction of intercourse pain than CBT and equal results for other pain- and sex-related outcomes

therapies_index.name: topical oestrogen
approved_indications: Considered for vulvodynia alone or with testosterone, but the data and recommendations conflict
therapies_index.administration: Topical; no schedule is given.

therapies_index.name: testosterone
approved_indications: Considered with topical oestrogen for vulvodynia, but the data and recommendations conflict
therapies_index.administration: No schedule is given.

therapies_index.name: vestibulectomy
approved_indications: Last-resort option for provoked vestibulodynia after failure of all available treatments, despite low-level evidence
therapies_index.administration: Posterior or total vestibulectomy, with or without vaginal advancement.
key_toxicities: Short- and long-term complications may include bleeding, wound dehiscence, Bartholin’s cyst and an unsatisfactory cosmetic appearance.

therapies_index.name: surgical cold knife excision
approved_indications: HSIL
DVIN
key_toxicities: Treatment of HSIL has high recurrence rates and may adversely affect quality of life and sexual function.
monitoring: Lifelong close follow-up is mandatory for VIN; HSIL review is every 6–12 months and DVIN review is at least every 6 months.

therapies_index.name: Laser CO2 therapy
approved_indications: HSIL
monitoring: Lifelong close follow-up for HSIL, every 6–12 months.

therapies_index.name: Loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP)
approved_indications: HSIL
monitoring: Lifelong close follow-up for HSIL, every 6–12 months.

therapies_index.name: Imiquimod cream
therapies_index.mechanism: Modifies the immune response and has indirect antiviral and antitumour properties.
approved_indications: HSIL
therapies_index.administration: Apply as a cream; no schedule is given.
monitoring: Lifelong close follow-up for HSIL, every 6–12 months.

therapies_index.name: therapeutic HPV vaccines
approved_indications: Developed with differing rates of clinical success; not yet available for routine clinical use

therapies_index.name: quadrivalent HPV 6/11/16/18
approved_indications: Prevention of HPV 16- and 18-related high-grade vulval and vaginal lesions in women negative for HPV 16 or 18 before vaccination
therapies_index.administration: Prophylactic vaccination; no schedule is given.

therapies_index.name: bivalent (16/18) vaccine
approved_indications: Prevention of HPV 16- and 18-related high-grade vulval and vaginal lesions in women negative for HPV 16 or 18 before vaccination
therapies_index.administration: Prophylactic vaccination; no schedule is given.

therapies_index.name: nonavalent vaccine
approved_indications: Prevention of HPV-related lesions; the guide reports slightly better prevention than the quadrivalent and bivalent vaccines
therapies_index.administration: Prophylactic vaccination; the listed types are HPV 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58. No schedule is given.

conditions.name: Vulval dermatitis (Eczema)
conditions.description: Inflammatory skin reaction with spongiosis, variable acanthosis and a superficial lymphohistiocytic infiltrate. Exogenous or endogenous factors may contribute. A specific diagnosis is preferable to using dermatitis or eczema as a general label for a pruritic red vulval eruption.
conditions.epidemiology: Irritant contact dermatitis is the form of eczema most commonly affecting the vulva.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Itch predominates; soreness and pain can occur. Findings include often symmetrical erythema of the labia that may extend to perianal skin or the gluteal cleft, excoriations, acute erosions, oozing or crusting, debris in the inter-labial sulci and, with chronicity, lichenification. Allergic contact dermatitis may extend onto the thighs. Secondary infection and lichen simplex chronicus can develop.

subtypes.name: Atopic dermatitis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Evidence increasingly implicates impaired skin-barrier function. Genital skin is spared in many affected people, although vulval lichen simplex chronicus can be an isolated manifestation or accompany disease elsewhere.

subtypes.name: Irritant contact dermatitis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Moisture, friction and topical products can aggravate vulval skin; urinary incontinence is a particular contributor.

subtypes.name: Allergic contact dermatitis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Delayed type IV hypersensitivity to an applied product, commonly a fragrance, antibiotic, local anaesthetic or topical-treatment component.

subtypes.name: Seborrhoeic dermatitis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Desquamative inflammatory disease primarily affecting the scalp and face. Vulval features can resemble psoriasis, but erythema is less sharply defined.

diagnostic_workup.test: Clinical history and examination of the vulva and remaining skin
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish the specific dermatitis diagnosis and look for atopic or seborrhoeic features and alternative causes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Well-demarcated plaques and fissures suggest psoriasis; a sharply bounded annular eruption with a papular or pustular, scaling edge suggests tinea cruris.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Clarify atypical or treatment-resistant disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If features are atypical or treatment fails.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate suspected contact allergy, including relevant medicaments, preservatives and products applied to the vulva.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When allergic contact dermatitis is suspected; testing is not needed for every form of dermatitis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A positive result does not by itself establish that the product caused the vulval eruption; a negative result does not definitively exclude a product. Clinical relevance requires careful assessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess candidiasis and exclude bacterial infection.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When infection is a possible alternative or concurrent diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help exclude tinea cruris.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When its clinical features raise suspicion.

follow_up.schedule: Routine review is unnecessary; review patients needing a stronger topical steroid or having difficulty controlling symptoms.
long_term_effects: Symptoms may recur.
Secondary infection or lichen simplex chronicus may develop.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Explain the possibility of recurrence and provide advice about hygiene practices that can aggravate symptoms.

conditions.name: Vulval psoriasis
conditions.description: Genital involvement in psoriasis, an immune-mediated disease with genetic predisposition. It may be localized or occur alongside more widespread psoriasis.
conditions.epidemiology: Psoriasis affects the genital area during life in up to 63% of patients. Adult psoriasis prevalence ranges from 0.5 to 11.4%, and isolated genital lesions occur in 2–5% of patients. Psoriatic arthritis occurs in 15–30% of patients with psoriasis vulgaris or exudative psoriasis.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Pruritus is reported most often; pain, burning and dyspareunia also occur. Vulval plaques are typically symmetrical, red and clearly bounded, sometimes extending to adjacent areas or accompanied by painful fissures. Fine silvery scale is less common genitally than elsewhere. Scalp and nail disease, inverse psoriasis, onset after 20 years of age and a higher Psoriasis Activity Score Index (PASI) are described as risk factors for vulval involvement.

subtypes.name: psoriasis vulgaris
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Genital disease may be localized or accompany plaques elsewhere, including extensor sites or the gluteal cleft.

subtypes.name: inverse psoriasis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: In rare cases, flexural-fold disease includes the genital area.

subtypes.name: Generalized pustular psoriasis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Pustules may begin on erythematous genital or other flexural areas before spreading over the body.

subtypes.name: Impetigo herpetiformis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Rare pregnancy-associated eruption with pustules arising in intertriginous areas, including the vulva; onset is typically in the last trimester, followed by rapid postpartum resolution.

subtypes.name: Erythrodermic psoriasis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Uncommon form that can affect more than 90% of the body surface, potentially including the vulva.

diagnostic_workup.test: Clinical history and examination, including scalp, nails, natal cleft and umbilicus
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify genital psoriasis and signs at other typical sites.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During diagnostic assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The combination of history and examination usually establishes the diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Further assess suspected psoriatic lesions.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When useful to clinical evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Dotted vessels or tortuous capillaries may be visible.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess characteristic tissue changes.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Findings described include parakeratosis, Munro micro-abscesses, absence of the granular layer, epidermal hyperplasia, frequent basal-layer mitoses and dilated tortuous capillaries in dermal papillae.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess possible associated conditions.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider when clinically appropriate.

prognostic_tools.name: Genital Psoriasis Symptoms Scale (GPSS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Patient-reported assessment of genital symptoms on a 11-point scale.

prognostic_tools.name: Static Physicians’ Global Assessment of Genitalia (sPGA-G)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Clinician assessment of genital signs on a 6-point scale.

prognostic_tools.name: Psoriasis Activity Score Index (PASI)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: A higher value is identified as a risk factor for vulval lesions.

follow_up.schedule: Assess active disease when clinically needed; review stable disease after 1–3 months.

conditions.name: Lichen simplex chronicus
conditions.description: Anogenital condition involving persistent itching and lichenification. It can arise on previously normal vulval skin or over another pruritic vulval disorder.
conditions.epidemiology: Estimated to affect approximately 0.5% of the Western European and American population and to account for 10–35% of vulval-clinic patients. It usually develops in mid- to late-adult life. Up to 75% of affected patients have a personal or immediate family history of atopy.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Severe persistent or intermittent itching commonly occurs in the evening or during sleep. Erosions or ulcers may cause burning, soreness and dyspareunia. Examination can show poorly defined thickened plaques, fissures, erosions, ulcers, pigment changes and broken hairs from rubbing. Secondary infection can occur; deep, prolonged scratching may permanently alter vulval architecture. An increased squamous cell cancer risk does not appear to be associated with vulval lichen simplex chronicus.

subtypes.name: Primary or idiopathic lichen simplex chronicus
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Develops on previously normal vulval skin, usually in a person with atopy.

subtypes.name: Secondary lichen simplex chronicus
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Occurs over an itchy condition such as eczema, psoriasis, lichen sclerosus or fungal or yeast infection.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess personal or first-degree family atopy, skin disease elsewhere and possible underlying causes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During diagnostic assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Examination is usually sufficient for diagnosis; disease elsewhere can help distinguish alternatives.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Clarify an uncertain diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Rarely, when clinical findings do not establish the diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Histopathology can have difficulty distinguishing this condition from psoriasis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate possible infection, including Staphylococcus aureus or Candida albicans.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When indicated clinically.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate suspected contact allergy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If contact allergy is suspected, with dermatological referral.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess suspected depleted iron stores.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For example, when a woman is vegetarian, donates blood regularly or has menorrhagia.

follow_up.schedule: Review mild disease when clinically needed. For severe disease requiring potent topical corticosteroids, review at 4 weeks and subsequently as needed.
long_term_effects: Secondary infection may occur.
Prolonged deep scratching can cause severe, irreversible architectural damage.

conditions.name: Lichen sclerosus
conditions.description: Chronic inflammatory skin disease predominantly involving anogenital rather than other skin sites. It typically spares the vagina and very rarely affects oral mucosa. Early recognition matters because treatment prevents scarring and may prevent malignant change; asymptomatic disease also requires treatment to prevent scarring.
conditions.epidemiology: Predominantly seen in adult women, although children may be affected. A study estimated incidence in women by age 80 at 1.6%. About 10% of patients with vulval LS have a reported positive family history, possibly an underestimate.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Possible findings include itch, soreness, dyspareunia or apareunia, urinary difficulties and, particularly in children with perianal disease, constipation; some patients have no symptoms. Pale white thickened or thinned areas, sclerosis, hyperkeratosis, purpura, fissures and erosions may affect the vulva alone or form a ‘figure-ofeight’ anogenital pattern. Scarring can resorb the labia minora and bury the clitoris without loss of the clitoris. Potential consequences include sexual or urinary dysfunction, dysaesthesia, clitoral pseudo-cyst and ano-genital squamous cell carcinoma, with actual risk <5%. Clitoral disease may start with preputial swelling before plaques, fissuring and fusion develop.

subtypes.name: Clitoral LS
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May appear confined to the clitoral hood, although other vulval areas are often involved; progressive fusion and scarring can affect function.

subtypes.name: Extragenital LS
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Affects skin outside the anogenital region; follicular plugging may be present.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify characteristic skin changes, including clitoral involvement and architectural loss.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During diagnostic assessment and monitoring.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Typical appearances may establish the diagnosis without biopsy.

diagnostic_workup.test: Biopsy of a typical lesion with clinical–histopathological correlation
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Resolve diagnostic uncertainty or assess suspected dysplasia or carcinoma.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If the clinical diagnosis is uncertain, dysplasia or carcinoma is suspected, or first-line treatment fails.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Findings include hyperkeratosis, epidermal atrophy, basal hydropic degeneration, a lymphohistiocytic infiltrate within a hyaline upper-dermal band with loss of elastic tissue, and possible follicular plugging. Early histology may be nonspecific.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess potentially associated conditions, including thyroid disease, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo and diabetes mellitus.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If clinically indicated; associated conditions can be asymptomatic.

diagnostic_workup.test: Skin swabs for bacterial, fungal or viral infection
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Exclude a concurrent infection.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Only when symptoms or signs suggest infection.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate suspected secondary allergy to a topical preparation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Rarely, if medicament allergy is suspected, including when a formerly effective preparation loses effect.

genetic_molecular.clinical_significance: Increased autoantibodies have been reported in LS, but their significance is unknown.
Increased autoantibodies to this antigen have been reported; their significance is unknown.
A possible contribution of mutations to vulval cancer arising in LS is postulated, not established.

follow_up.schedule: Assess treatment response after 3 months. Review stable disease annually; a GP may perform this review when disease is well controlled, provided the specialist communicates the plan to both patient and GP.
recommended_tests: Clinical review of response and changes in lesion appearance or symptoms.
long_term_effects: Scarring and loss of vulval architecture.
Ano-genital squamous cell carcinoma, with actual risk <5%.
Sexual and urinary dysfunction.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Patients should seek prompt assessment for a new lump or sore area, altered appearance, or a change in symptoms. Disease inadequately controlled by treatment warrants specialist referral; VIN or SCC arising with LS requires experienced specialist follow-up.

conditions.name: Lichen planus
conditions.description: Inflammatory disorder that can affect the skin, hair, nails, genital and oral mucosa and, less commonly, other mucosal sites. Vulval disease has classical, hypertrophic and erosive presentations; LP and LS may coexist.
conditions.epidemiology: Vulval LP accounted for 8.8% of patients attending a tertiary-hospital dermatology clinic in a cited review. In a study of 37 women with cutaneous LP, 19 had vulval lesions, including four of the 19 without symptoms.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Possible symptoms are irritation or itching, soreness, dyspareunia, urinary complaints and vaginal discharge, although disease can be asymptomatic. Scarring, particularly vaginal synechiae with erosive disease, may occur. A prospective study following 114 patients for a mean of six years reported vulval intraepithelial neoplasia in seven and anogenital SCC in two (1.8%). The document states that whether early treatment or sustained disease control reduces malignancy risk is unknown.

subtypes.name: Classical
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Papules on keratinized anogenital skin may show Wickham’s striae; pigmentation can follow resolution, particularly in dark skin.

subtypes.name: Hypertrophic
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Uncommon thickened, wart-like perineal or perianal plaques can ulcerate, become infected or painful and resemble malignancy; vaginal lesions are usually absent.

subtypes.name: Erosive
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The vulval subtype most likely to cause symptoms; eroded mucosa may be accompanied by vaginal disease, friable telangiectasias, discharge and subsequent adhesions or stenosis.

diagnostic_workup.test: Clinical examination of vulval and other potentially affected mucosal or skin sites
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the distribution and subtype of LP and distinguish other causes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During initial assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Vaginal involvement practically excludes lichen sclerosus, which typically spares non-keratinized mucosa.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Support clinical identification of LP.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When additional assessment is helpful.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Possible features include diffusely arranged thick irregular linear vessels, peripheral Wickham’s striae and an intensely red background.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Clarify uncertain disease or investigate possible coexisting intraepithelial neoplasia or SCC.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If clinical diagnosis is uncertain or neoplasia is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Classical LP can show irregular ‘saw-tooth’ acanthosis, an increased granular layer, basal-cell liquefaction and a predominantly lymphocytic band-like dermal infiltrate. Histology may be nonspecific; only 25% of biopsies are classic.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate an immunobullous alternative.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If an immunobullous disorder is in the differential diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess suspected thyroid or other autoimmune disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Only if clinical findings suggest an abnormality.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Exclude secondary infection.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Particularly for excoriated lesions.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess possible contact allergy to a medicament.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If medicament contact allergy is suspected.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess possible hepatitis infection.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be prudent in populations with high viral-hepatitis prevalence; routine screening was considered unnecessary by the cited UK study.

follow_up.schedule: Review treatment response at 2–3 months and active disease as clinically needed. Review stable disease annually, except for well-counselled patients controlling symptoms well. Erosive disease requires long-term specialist follow-up.
recommended_tests: Clinical assessment of disease activity and changes in vulval lesions.
long_term_effects: Vulval or vaginal scarring and synechiae.
Possible neoplastic change; whether treatment lowers this risk is unknown.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Advise urgent assessment of a new lump, skin hardening or persistent ulcer. A GP-led review plan should be communicated to the patient and GP.

conditions.name: erosive LP
conditions.description: Mucosal form of LP that may involve the vulva, vagina or oral cavity. Vaginal involvement can occur without vulval disease, making early identification important to limit scarring and stenosis.
conditions.epidemiology: In a series of 114 women with erosive LP, the mean age at onset of vulval symptoms was 56.9 years.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Pain and soreness commonly accompany mucosal erosions bordered by red-to-purple epithelium and sometimes Wickham’s striae. Vaginal inflammation may cause dyspareunia, postcoital bleeding and often serosanguinous discharge. Healing may produce adhesions, scarring or complete vaginal stenosis. Erosive disease across vulval, vaginal and gingival sites is termed vulvo–vaginal–gingival syndrome.

diagnostic_workup.test: Proposed clinical and histological diagnostic criteria
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Support diagnosis of vulval erosive LP.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When erosive LP is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An international e-Delphi exercise suggested that at least three criteria be present: sharply defined introital erosions or erythema; a hyperkeratotic edge or surrounding Wickham striae; pain or burning; scarring or architectural loss; vaginal inflammation; involvement of another mucosal surface; a well-defined inflammatory band at the dermo-epidermal junction; a predominantly lymphocytic inflammatory band; or basal-layer degeneration.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Differentiate suspected vulval LP from vulvar LS and chronic vulvovaginal candidiasis in a cited study.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In the study's assessment of clinically suspected vulval LP.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The study identified erosions, glazed erythema, oral involvement, pain or burning, and a hyperkeratotic border as discriminating features. A score ≥2 correlated with histopathological vulvar LP, with sensitivity 100% and specificity 92% against vulvar LS and 88% against chronic vulvovaginal candidiasis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Clarify uncertain diagnosis or assess possible intraepithelial neoplasia or SCC.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When the clinical diagnosis is uncertain or coexistent neoplasia is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Possible findings are pronounced epithelial apoptosis, lymphocytic inflammation, plasma cells and ulceration, with more typical LP changes at the ulcer edge. Clinical–histopathological correlation remains important.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess a possible immunobullous disorder.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If such a disorder is considered in the differential diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Exclude secondary infection.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Especially when lesions are excoriated.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate suspected medicament contact allergy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If contact allergy is suspected.

follow_up.schedule: Assess treatment response at 2–3 months; thereafter assess active disease when clinically necessary and provide long-term specialist follow-up.
recommended_tests: Clinical evaluation of vulval and vaginal activity, scarring and concerning lesion changes.
long_term_effects: Vaginal synechiae, scarring and possible complete stenosis.
Potential neoplastic change.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Referral to a multidisciplinary vulval clinic is recommended for erosive disease. Advise urgent assessment of a lump, hardening or persistent ulcer.

conditions.name: Hypertrophic
conditions.description: Relatively uncommon clinical presentation of vulval LP involving thickened lesions that can resemble malignancy.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Thickened wart-like plaques principally affect the perineum and perianal skin. They may ulcerate, become infected and cause pain. Vaginal lesions are not usually present.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess thickened lesions and possible malignant mimics.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During evaluation of suspected hypertrophic LP.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Clinical resemblance to malignancy can make diagnosis difficult.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Clarify uncertain diagnosis or assess suspected coexistent intraepithelial neoplasia or SCC.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If diagnosis is clinically uncertain or neoplasia is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: On keratinized skin, basal-layer degeneration is particularly helpful for distinguishing LP from nodular prurigo or lichenified psoriasis, although superinfection can obscure or mimic it. Pseudo-epitheliomatous hyperplasia may resemble microinvasive SCC.

follow_up.schedule: Assess response at 2–3 months, review active disease as clinically needed and stable disease annually, subject to the guide's exception for well-counselled patients with good symptom control.
long_term_effects: Lesions can resemble malignancy; differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia may superficially resemble hypertrophic LP.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Advise urgent review for a new lump, hardening or persistent ulcer.

conditions.name: Vulvodynia
conditions.description: Vulvar pain lasting at least 3 months without a clearly identifiable cause, although associated factors may be present. The document describes altered peripheral and central sensory processing and classifies symptoms by distribution and provocation.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Pain is often described as burning but may involve stinging, tingling, rawness or irritation. It can be spontaneous, contact-provoked or both, and localized or widespread. Sexual or nonsexual contact may trigger pain; vestibular pain can make penetration difficult. The vulva has no finding that adequately explains the discomfort. Gentle cotton-applicator pressure can elicit pain in provoked vestibulodynia, while neurological examination remains normal. Psychological and sexual well-being may be substantially affected.

subtypes.name: generalized
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Discomfort involves the whole vulva and may extend toward the thighs or perianal region.

subtypes.name: localized
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Pain is confined to a vulval region, most often the vestibule.

subtypes.name: vestibulodynia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Localized vestibular discomfort, particularly posteriorly; provoked vestibulodynia is described as the most reproducible subset.

subtypes.name: clitorodynia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Less common discomfort localized to the clitoris.

subtypes.name: provoked
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Sexual contact or nonsexual contact, such as tampon insertion or examination, brings on discomfort.

subtypes.name: unprovoked
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Pain occurs spontaneously rather than being elicited by touch.

subtypes.name: mixed
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Spontaneous pain is also aggravated by sexual or nonsexual contact.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish a clinical diagnosis and exclude another explanation for vulvar discomfort.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During diagnostic assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A visible lesion does not establish the cause of pain unless it adequately explains the symptom pattern.

diagnostic_workup.test: Gentle vestibular pressure with a cotton tipped applicator
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess contact-provoked vestibular tenderness.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When provoked vestibulodynia is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Pressure elicits vestibular tenderness or pain.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess for objective abnormalities suggesting another cause of perineal pain.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During assessment and particularly if a neurological alternative is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Examination is normal in vulvodynia; objective abnormalities, sphincter disturbance or unilateral or diffuse pain raise concern for a neurological condition such as pudendal neuralgia.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Exclude a compressive process when assessing a possible neurological cause.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If findings suggest a neurological alternative such as pudendal neuralgia.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help assess a possible neurological cause of perineal pain.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If a neurological differential diagnosis is suspected.

prognostic_tools.name: OPQRST
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Mnemonic for describing vulvar discomfort; the document does not assign risk categories.

follow_up.schedule: Multidisciplinary long-term follow-up, every 3 months until improvement.
long_term_effects: Possible continuing effects on psychological and sexual well-being.
Significant improvement or complete remission may occur spontaneously or after treatment.

conditions.name: HSIL
conditions.description: One of the premalignant vulval entities in the ISSVD terminology; associated with persistent high-risk Human Papilloma Virus (HPV) infection. It differs from DVIN in cause, malignant potential and management.
conditions.epidemiology: Incidence is approximately 5 per 100 000 women per year and is increasing; the highest peak occurs between 35 and 49 years. Smoking and immuno-compromised status are risk factors.
conditions.clinical_presentation: May cause itch, burning, irritation, pain or psychosexual complaints, or be asymptomatic. Appearance varies: plaques may be white, red or pigmented, and lesions may be multifocal. SCC development, recurrence after treatment and psychosexual difficulties are possible.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish diagnosis across potentially multifocal disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When HSIL or DVIN is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Histology can show disrupted squamous-epithelial organization, cytological atypia, a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and mitotic figures.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Distinguish HSIL from dVIN.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During pathological differentiation of these entities.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: HSIL is p16 positive and shows normal p53.

pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Marker of HPV positivity that helps distinguish HSIL from dVIN.
The reported pattern helps differentiate HSIL from dVIN.

genetic_molecular.clinical_significance: Persistent infection with high-risk HPV causes HSIL.

definitions.description: High-grade squamous intraepithelial vulval lesion in the terminology accepted by ISSVD in 2015.

staging.additional_rules: The document treats HSIL and DVIN as distinct premalignant entities; it does not provide a numerical staging system for HSIL.

follow_up.schedule: Close lifelong follow-up, with HSIL review every 6–12 months.
long_term_effects: Possible vulval squamous cell carcinoma.
High recurrence rate after treatment.
Psychosexual complaints.

conditions.name: DVIN
conditions.description: HPV-independent premalignant vulval lesion associated with LS and LP. Its malignant potential is higher than that of HSIL.
conditions.epidemiology: Occurs mainly in older women and represents less than 5% of VIN lesions.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Symptoms often arise from underlying lichen sclerosus or lichen planus. Lesions can be difficult to distinguish from lichen sclerosus and may be grey-white or red, with a roughened or ulcerated surface. They are more often unifocal than HSIL. SCC development and recurrence after treatment are possible.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify disease and evaluate each suspicious lesion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When VIN is suspected; histopathological diagnosis of DVIN can be difficult.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Described findings include hyperplasia, hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, elongated and interconnected rete ridges, basal atypia, prominent nucleoli, atypical basal mitoses, dyskeratosis and maturation of rete ridges.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Differentiate dVIN from HSIL.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During pathological assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: dVIN is p16 negative and shows mutations in the p53 gene.

pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Helps distinguish HPV-independent dVIN from HSIL.
The reported finding helps differentiate dVIN from HSIL.

genetic_molecular.clinical_significance: DVIN is described as independent of HPV.
The document reports mutations in the p53 gene in dVIN, in contrast to normal p53 in HSIL.

definitions.description: Differentiated-type vulval intraepithelial neoplasia in the terminology accepted by ISSVD in 2015.

staging.additional_rules: The document distinguishes DVIN from HSIL and does not provide a numerical staging system.

follow_up.schedule: Close lifelong follow-up; the interval depends on underlying disease but is at least every 6 months.
long_term_effects: Risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma, with higher malignant potential than HSIL.
High recurrence rate after treatment.
Psychosexual complaints.

special_populations.population: Pregnant or breastfeeding patients with vulval psoriasis
special_populations.considerations: Emollients are considered safe during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Pregnant and breastfeeding patients were excluded from the cited studies of topical corticosteroids and vitamin D analogues, and information on medication excretion into breast milk is unavailable. Short-term topical coal tar use during pregnancy is considered to carry only a small risk. Impetigo herpetiformis can arise in pregnancy, typically during the last trimester, and usually resolves rapidly after delivery.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Topical calcineurin inhibitors are not licensed during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Treatment with ustekinumab, secukinumab, ixekizumab and guselkumab should be avoided during pregnancy. Use of these biologic agents while breastfeeding requires an assessment of risks and benefits for the child and mother.

special_populations.considerations: In patients with HIV, psoriasis may occur more often, show atypical forms and resist treatment.

special_populations.population: Patients with urinary incontinence and vulval dermatitis
special_populations.considerations: Urine exposure makes irritant contact dermatitis a particular concern in this group.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Address the incontinence; referral to uro-gynaecology may be helpful. Barrier preparations are particularly useful when incontinence is substantial.

special_populations.population: Patients with an atopic diathesis and lichen simplex chronicus
special_populations.considerations: Anogenital lichen simplex chronicus occurs most often in people with an atopic background; up to 75% have a personal or immediate family history of atopy. Primary disease can arise on otherwise normal vulval skin, whereas secondary disease overlies another pruritic vulval condition.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Identify any underlying disease when managing lichen simplex chronicus.

special_populations.considerations: Lichen sclerosus can affect children. Perianal involvement may cause symptoms such as constipation.

Retinoids are absolutely contraindicated during pregnancy and for at least 2 years before conception, and require caution in females of child-bearing age.

special_populations.considerations: Disease may be confined to the clitoral hood, although other vulval areas are often involved. Early swelling can progress to white plaques, fissures, fusion and scarring. Mechanical irritation may help sustain disease.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Examine for clitoral involvement and treat it as lichen sclerosus at other genital sites. Avoid mechanical triggers and massage topical preparations in gently. Surgery for fusion is indicated only rarely, such as for severe effects on self-esteem, sexual function or urination; it requires an experienced surgeon and counselling about adverse effects and recurrence.

special_populations.population: Pregnant or breastfeeding patients with lichen planus

special_populations.population: Patients with erosive lichen planus involving the vagina
special_populations.considerations: Vaginal involvement may occur without vulval disease and can lead to scarring or complete stenosis. Erosive disease may also affect the vulva and gingiva.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Recognize vaginal involvement and begin treatment early. Vaginal corticosteroids may be delivered as ointment on a tampon overnight, hydrocortisone rectal foam introduced vaginally 1–2 times daily, or prednisolone suppositories in more severe cases. Erosive vulval disease warrants referral to a multidisciplinary vulval clinic and long-term specialist follow-up.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The cited multicentre comparative trial closed without reaching its recruitment target. TNF-a inhibitors have been reported to induce LP-like eruptions, including erosive oral and vulval disease, so their use is reserved for only the most recalcitrant cases. basiliximab was reported effective in a single severe erosive oral LP case but has not been evaluated for vulval disease.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with a severe flare or hypertrophic disease
decision_rules: Consider a short course of oral steroid for severe flares.
The retinoid acitretin may help hypertrophic disease.

alternative_regimens.name: prednisolone
alternative_regimens.summary: An oral steroid example for severe flares, given at 40 mg/day and tapered; courses may be repeated when necessary.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Severe flares; taper over a few weeks

alternative_regimens.name: acitretin
alternative_regimens.summary: May help hypertrophic LP; it is severely teratogenic.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Hypertrophic disease; pregnancy is contraindicated and must be avoided for 2 years after treatment

not_recommended.name: acitretin during pregnancy
not_recommended.reason: Absolutely contraindicated because of severe teratogenicity.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Use acitretin cautiously in other females of child-bearing age.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with symptomatic vulval or vaginal adhesions and scarring
decision_rules: Consider surgery for symptomatic adhesions and scarring only when active inflammatory disease is absent.
Use a potent topical steroid immediately after surgical adhesiolysis.

recommended_regimens.name: Potent topical steroids
recommended_regimens.summary: Use routinely immediately after surgical adhesiolysis to improve long-term outcomes and function.

alternative_regimens.name: Surgical lysis of vulvo–vaginal adhesions
alternative_regimens.summary: In a study of 11 women with LP scarring, surgery permitted intercourse in 55% and reduced urination difficulties in 75%; 91% were satisfied and would recommend it. Sexual difficulties can nevertheless persist.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Symptomatic adhesions or scarring without active inflammatory disease

not_recommended.name: Surgery during active inflammatory disease
not_recommended.reason: Contraindicated.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Pregnant or breastfeeding patients
decision_rules: Topical steroids are described as safe during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

recommended_regimens.name: Topical steroids
recommended_regimens.summary: May be used during pregnancy or breastfeeding.

not_recommended.name: Topical calcineurin inhibitors
not_recommended.reason: Not licensed during pregnancy or breastfeeding.

not_recommended.name: Retinoids
not_recommended.reason: Absolutely contra-indicated during pregnancy and for at least 2 years before conception.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Retinoids should be used cautiously in females of child-bearing age.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with vulvodynia
decision_rules: Use a multidimensional approach to chronic vulval pain while recognizing that supporting evidence levels are low.
Physical therapy is considered first-line treatment; psychosexual interventions are also recommended.
Avoid irritants and use emulsifying ointments and soap substitutes.

recommended_regimens.name: Physical therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Rehabilitates pelvic floor muscle function and desensitizes painful vulval tissue through education, exercises with biofeedback, manual therapy or dilation, alone or combined. Clinicians experienced in chronic vulval pain and its sexual effects obtain the best results.

recommended_regimens.name: Psychosexual interventions
recommended_regimens.summary: Includes cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT), pain management, sex therapy and psychoeducation, offered alone or together. These interventions address pain, sexual function, well-being and relationship effects.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Studies reported that CBT improved intercourse pain as much as vestibulectomy and outperformed topical corticosteroids and supportive psychotherapy for pain reduction and sexual functioning. Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) reduced intercourse pain more than CBT and had equal results for other pain- and sex-related outcomes.

alternative_regimens.name: Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve stimulation (TENS)
alternative_regimens.summary: Can be self-administered and is best incorporated into multidimensional care.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: As part of a multidimensional strategy

alternative_regimens.name: Acupuncture
alternative_regimens.summary: Small clinical trials reported improvements in pain and sexual functioning, alone or with lidocaine; study protocols are being improved.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consideration of an additional intervention

alternative_regimens.name: Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT)
alternative_regimens.summary: A psychosexual approach studied alongside CBT; women with high credibility about mindfulness, shorter relationships or secondary PVD might respond better than with CBT.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selection of a suitable psychosexual intervention

not_recommended.name: Surgery as routine treatment for vulvodynia
not_recommended.reason: Surgery is usually not recommended for chronic pain involving dysfunctional pain processing.

supportive_care: Name the condition, affirm that the pain is real and explain its possible effects on quality of life.
Give verbal and written information about current understanding of mechanisms, contributing factors, treatment and prognosis.
Lifestyle advice may form part of multidimensional care, although evidence specific to women with vulvodynia is lacking.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Recommendations for stopping combined hormonal contraception or adding topical oestrogen, alone or with testosterone, conflict. A substantial placebo effect complicates interpretation of vulvodynia treatment studies.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with introital dyspareunia due to provoked vestibulodynia
decision_rules: Local anaesthetics are mainly prescribed for provoked vestibulodynia-associated introital dyspareunia.
Distinguish application before intercourse from prolonged daily use, which was not more effective than placebo for vestibular pain.

alternative_regimens.name: 5% lidocaine ointment
alternative_regimens.summary: A topical pain modifier applied before penetrative sex and washed off immediately before penetration.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Introital dyspareunia due to provoked vestibulodynia; apply 10–20 min before penetrative sex

alternative_regimens.name: 2% lidocaine gel
alternative_regimens.summary: A topical pain modifier applied before penetrative sex and washed off immediately before penetration.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Introital dyspareunia due to provoked vestibulodynia; apply 10–20 min before penetrative sex

not_recommended.name: Long-term daily Lidocaine 5%
not_recommended.reason: Application four times a day for 12 weeks was not more effective than placebo for reducing vestibular pain.

not_recommended.name: Botulinum neurotoxin
not_recommended.reason: Injections of 20–50 units into the bulbo-cavernosus muscles were not superior to placebo for pain reduction.

not_recommended.name: 0.025% to 0.05% capsaicin cream
not_recommended.reason: Benefit has not been demonstrated, and burning limits use.

not_recommended.name: Cannabis
not_recommended.reason: Evidence is currently insufficient to recommend it for vulvodynia.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Topical pain modifiers are assigned GRADE 2. Further investigation is needed to establish the efficacy of 2% amitryptiline cream, alone or with baclofen.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients considered for oral pain modifiers, particularly those with generalized unprovoked vulvodynia
decision_rules: Evidence does not adequately support the benefit of tricyclic antidepressants despite their widespread use.
Discuss the specific trial findings and tolerability limitations of oral agents.

alternative_regimens.name: Amitriptyline
alternative_regimens.summary: Frequently used at 5 to 50 mg daily, but two small RCT studies of low or moderate quality did not confirm efficacy; tolerance is often poor.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consideration of an oral pain modifier, particularly for generalized unprovoked vulvodynia, acknowledging insufficient evidence of benefit

alternative_regimens.name: milnacipran
alternative_regimens.summary: Oral treatment at 50–200 mg per day reduced coital pain in a reported study.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consideration of an oral pain modifier; the reported treatment lasted 12 weeks

not_recommended.name: Desimipramine
not_recommended.reason: Increasing the dose from 25 mg to 150 mg over 12 weeks was not superior to placebo.

not_recommended.name: Gabapentin
not_recommended.reason: At 1200 to 3000 mg per day it was not more effective than placebo for tampon-test pain or dyspareunia, although a positive effect on sexual function, particularly arousal, was reported.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Oral pain modifiers are assigned GRADE 2. Evidence for pregabalin is limited.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with provoked vestibulodynia after failure of all available therapeutic options
decision_rules: Consider vestibulectomy only as a last-resort intervention, despite the low level of evidence.

alternative_regimens.name: vestibulectomy
alternative_regimens.summary: Posterior or total surgery, with or without vaginal advancement, has been reported to provide lasting reduction of introital dyspareunia and patient satisfaction. Sexual-function results were moderate or not superior to electromyographic biofeedback or CBT.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Provoked vestibulodynia after all available therapeutic options have failed

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Possible short- and long-term complications include bleeding, wound dehiscence, Bartholin’s cyst and unsatisfactory cosmetic appearance.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with HSIL
treatment_pathways.biomarker_condition: HSIL is HPV driven and p16 positive.
decision_rules: Biopsy every lesion to map disease before treatment.
Discuss surgical and imiquimod options, taking account of frequent recurrence and the potential effects of surgery on quality of life and sexual function.
Lifelong close follow-up is mandatory.

recommended_regimens.name: Surgical cold knife excision
recommended_regimens.summary: A listed treatment; surgery has traditionally been the first choice, although recurrence is common and quality of life and sexual function can be adversely affected.

recommended_regimens.name: Imiquimod cream
recommended_regimens.summary: A newer topical treatment modality for HSIL.

alternative_regimens.name: Laser CO2 therapy
alternative_regimens.summary: A listed treatment for HSIL.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: HSIL treatment selection

alternative_regimens.name: Loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP)
alternative_regimens.summary: A listed treatment for HSIL.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: HSIL treatment selection

alternative_regimens.name: Follow up without treatment
alternative_regimens.summary: A listed option in view of possible spontaneous regression.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selected HSIL cases considered for observation

not_recommended.name: Therapeutic HPV vaccines for routine clinical use
not_recommended.reason: Therapeutic vaccines are not yet available for routine clinical use.

response_assessment.method: Clinical follow-up, with an annual cervical smear.
response_assessment.interpretation: Monitor for recurrence and vulval squamous cell carcinoma.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline assigns GRADE 1 to biopsy of all lesions. Prophylactic HPV vaccines are described as preventing HPV 16- and 18-related high-grade vulval and vaginal lesions in women negative for HPV 16 or 18 before vaccination; they are distinct from treatment of established HSIL.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with DVIN
treatment_pathways.biomarker_condition: DVIN is HPV independent and p16 negative; mutations in the p53 gene are described.
decision_rules: Biopsy every lesion to map disease.
Treat DVIN with surgical cold knife excision.
Plan lifelong close follow-up according to the underlying disease, at least every 6 months.

recommended_regimens.name: Surgical cold knife excision
recommended_regimens.summary: The listed treatment for DVIN.

response_assessment.method: Close clinical follow-up adapted to the underlying disease.
response_assessment.interpretation: Monitor for recurrence and vulval squamous cell carcinoma.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: DVIN is associated with LS and LP and has greater malignant potential than HSIL. The guideline assigns GRADE 1 to biopsy of all lesions.

recommendations.statement: Manage women with vulval conditions through a multidisciplinary approach, with clear referral routes between specialties or access to a specialist multidisciplinary vulval service.
recommendations.rationale: Assessment and treatment may involve several clinical specialties.
recommendations.source_heading: General advice for delivery of vulval care

recommendations.statement: Provide access to clinico-pathological review and discussion of histology findings.
recommendations.source_heading: General advice for delivery of vulval care
