recommendations.statement: Obtain informed consent before examinations, investigations and treatments; offer a chaperone for every examination and document the offer.
recommendations.context: Intimate anogenital examinations require particular attention to consent.

recommendations.statement: Explain the examination before the patient undresses, protect privacy and dignity, and ensure that appropriate equipment and a suitable examination room are available.
recommendations.context: Physical examination of patients with vulval symptoms

recommendations.statement: Consider STI screening in every patient according to symptoms and risk factors.
Exclude vulvovaginal candidiasis when vulval itch is present, particularly if discharge has increased.

If anti-candidal treatment does not relieve symptoms, especially when candida cultures are negative, perform a complete genital examination including speculum examination unless one was done recently, and consider other causes.
Consider sexual dysfunction in all patients and assess it when appropriate.
recommendations.context: Sexual dysfunction may precede symptoms or arise because of them.

recommendations.statement: When genital ulcers are present, test for herpes simplex and syphilis even if an ulcerating dermatosis is also present.
Investigate for concurrent STIs when lesions fail to heal with standard treatment.
Consider HIV testing in all patients, particularly when skin disorders have atypical features, numerous hyperkeratotic warts, treatment-resistant seborrheic dermatitis, or new or severe psoriasis.
recommendations.rationale: Skin disease may be an early manifestation of HIV-related immunosuppression.

recommendations.statement: Advise patients to avoid soap, shampoo, bubble bath and tight-fitting clothing; simple emollients may serve as soap substitutes and moisturizers.
recommendations.rationale: These exposures may irritate vulval skin.
recommendations.source_heading: General advice for all vulval conditions

recommendations.statement: Advise against condoms with spermicidal lubricant or local anaesthetics.
recommendations.source_heading: General advice for all vulval conditions

recommendations.statement: Explain the diagnosis and its possible long-term health implications in detail, provide accurate written information, and seek consent to inform the patient's GP about diagnosis and management.
recommendations.source_heading: General advice for all vulval conditions

recommendations.statement: Prefer ointment-based topical treatments for anogenital skin and consider regular barrier-emollient application to affected areas.
recommendations.context: Choice of topical vehicle and protection from irritants
recommendations.rationale: Ointments generally need fewer preservatives and carry less risk of secondary contact allergy; creams may sting, while a barrier may protect against urine and menstrual blood.

recommendations.statement: Do not undertake partner tracing unless screening identifies an STI.
Use a specific diagnosis, such as atopic dermatitis or irritant/allergic contact dermatitis, rather than applying the nonspecific labels dermatitis or eczema to every itchy erythematous condition.
recommendations.rationale: Other vulval conditions may also cause erythema and pruritus.

recommendations.statement: Perform a biopsy when features are atypical or the condition does not respond to treatment.
Perform patch testing when allergic contact dermatitis is suspected, in a clinic competent to conduct the investigation and interpret its results.
recommendations.context: Patch testing is not required for every form of dermatitis.

recommendations.statement: For suspected vulval allergic contact dermatitis, test the standard baseline allergen series as well as medicaments, preservatives and products the patient has applied to the vulva, using appropriate dilutions; assess the relevance of results carefully.
recommendations.context: A positive result does not establish that a product caused the rash, and a negative result does not completely exclude it.

recommendations.statement: Avoid suspected irritants and allergens, including cleansers, fragrances and wet wipes; address urinary incontinence when present and consider uro-gynaecology referral.
recommendations.rationale: These exposures may precipitate symptoms, while incontinence increases local irritation.

recommendations.statement: Use a bland emollient, such as emulsifying ointment, instead of soap; barrier preparations are particularly helpful with significant urinary incontinence.

For mild disease, topical 1% hydrocortisone ointment can be used; for more severe disease, mometasone furoate or betamethasone valerate 0.025% can be used once daily for 7–10 days until symptoms and signs resolve, then as needed for recurrence.
Treat coexisting infection with a steroid/antifungal or steroid/antibacterial combination.
Antihistamines may be used to help with disturbed sleep.
Topical tacrolimus or pimecrolimus may be tried for resistant disease as unlicensed treatments.
recommendations.context: Application may sting, although this can diminish with continued use.

recommendations.statement: Routine follow-up is unnecessary, but review patients requiring a more potent topical steroid or having difficulty controlling symptoms.
Explain the possibility of recurrent symptoms and advise patients about hygiene practices that may worsen the condition.
Avoid known triggers, including scented detergents, synthetic underwear and tight pants.
Use topical treatment for localized vulval disease; systemic treatment given for disseminated or generalized psoriasis also treats genital lesions.
Avoid anthralin, tazarotene and ultraviolet therapy for vulval psoriasis.
recommendations.rationale: Local adverse reactions, mainly irritation, may occur.

recommendations.statement: Present therapeutic options to the patient to choose an acceptable individualized regimen; where pubic hair is present, prefer solutions, foams or gels for vulval lesions.

Use topical corticosteroids in sequential or rotational regimens, with mid-potency preparations followed by low-potency preparations; determine duration and frequency according to the chosen steroid and clinical response.
Use topical vitamin D analogues alone or together with topical corticosteroids.
Coal tar preparations, such as 1–5% liquor carbonis detergens in aqueous cream, are suggested alone or with topical corticosteroids.
Use emollients to lessen irritation from other topical treatments and help maintain treatment results.

Systemic therapies, including methotrexate, retinoids, cyclosporine and biological agents, may be used for disseminated or generalized psoriasis involving the genitals or genital disease refractory to topical regimens.
Assess active disease as clinically needed and review stable disease after 1–3 months.
During pregnancy, avoid ustekinumab, secukinumab, ixekizumab and guselkumab; base decisions about their use during breastfeeding on an assessment of risks and benefits for the child and mother.
Improve skin barrier function with saline soaks followed, and subsequently replaced, by unperfumed lubricants; avoid petroleum-based lubricants.
recommendations.rationale: Petroleum-based lubricants are considered too greasy.

recommendations.statement: Identify any underlying disease.

For severe disease, prescribe a superpotent topical corticosteroid such as clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment once or twice daily, tapering slowly after improvement; for milder disease, fluticasone propionate 0.005% or mometasone furoate 0.1% ointment once or twice daily may be prescribed and tapered once improvement occurs.
An intralesional triamcinolone injection may be given for very thick plaques.
Intermittent ice application may help, but advise patients to limit each application to a maximum of 15 min.
recommendations.rationale: Longer application risks cold injury.

recommendations.statement: For scratching at night, consider a sedative antihistamine such as hydroxyzine or a tricyclic antidepressant such as amitriptyline.
Topical pimecrolimus 1% cream or tacrolimus 0.1% ointment twice daily for up to 12 weeks may be used as unlicensed second-line treatment.
Review mild disease as clinically needed; for severe disease requiring potent topical corticosteroids, review at 4 weeks and subsequently as needed.
Treat lichen sclerosus even when it causes no symptoms.
recommendations.rationale: Treatment aims to prevent scarring.

recommendations.statement: Perform a biopsy if the clinical diagnosis is uncertain, dysplasia or carcinoma is suspected, or first-line treatment fails.
recommendations.context: A biopsy may be unnecessary in typical cases; clinical and histopathological findings must be correlated.
recommendations.rationale: Histology may be nonspecific in early disease.

recommendations.statement: Investigate for autoimmune disease when clinically indicated; use bacterial, fungal or viral swabs to exclude coexisting infection only when suggestive symptoms or signs are present.
Reserve patch testing for suspected secondary medicament allergy and seek dermatology advice.
recommendations.rationale: Patch testing is rarely required.

recommendations.statement: Give patients written information, explain the small risk of neoplastic change, and advise them to contact a doctor about a new lump, ulceration, skin hardening, other change in appearance or texture, or a major symptom change.
Advise emollient use and avoidance of genital skin irritation, including irritating cleansing practices and exposure associated with incontinence.
recommendations.rationale: Emollients may relieve symptoms after initial steroid treatment.

recommendations.statement: Use ultra-potent or potent topical steroids, such as clobetasol proprionate or mometasone furoate, as first-line treatment for genital disease.

A commonly used initial regimen applies a potent to ultra-potent topical steroid, usually once daily, for three months; another applies it daily for one month, on alternate days for one month, and twice weekly for one month, with review at 3 months.
recommendations.context: The latter regimen may be preferred for children to avoid skin atrophy; twice-daily application may occasionally add benefit in resistant disease.

recommendations.statement: Use proactive twice-weekly maintenance treatment, for example mometasone furoate 0.1% ointment or clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment.
recommendations.context: Thirty grams of an ultra-potent steroid should last at least 3 months.
recommendations.rationale: This maintenance approach is described as effective and safe for sustaining remission and may help prevent malignant change.

recommendations.statement: If secondary infection is a concern, a potent or ultra-potent topical steroid combined with antibacterial and antifungal agents, or another preparation addressing the infection, may be appropriate; limit its use to the short period needed to clear infection.
Consider allergy testing if a previously effective topical preparation loses its effect.
recommendations.context: Possible allergy to a component of treatment
recommendations.rationale: Allergy to components, including steroids, may develop with long-term use.

recommendations.statement: Systemic retinoids such as aciretin may be considered after standard treatment fails, but should be prescribed only by a dermatologist experienced with these agents; avoid pregnancy for at least 2 years after treatment ends.
recommendations.rationale: The supporting trials are small and not of very high quality, and retinoids are severely teratogenic.

recommendations.statement: UVA1 phototherapy may be considered if topical corticosteroids fail.
recommendations.rationale: Carcinoma development documented after PUVA and UVB raises particular concern at genital sites.

recommendations.statement: Reserve vulval surgery for coexisting VIN/SCC or fusion.
recommendations.rationale: In females, disease tends to recur around the scar.

recommendations.statement: Do not currently recommend Adipose-Derived Stem Cells (ADSC) and/or Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) for vulvar disease.
recommendations.rationale: Current supporting evidence is weak.

recommendations.statement: Look for clitoral involvement and treat it as disease at other genital sites; advise avoidance of suspected mechanical triggers and gentle massage of topical preparations.

Operate on clitoral fusion only in rare circumstances, such as severe effects on self-esteem, sexual function or urination; use an experienced surgeon and counsel carefully about the procedure, adverse effects and possible recurrence.
recommendations.rationale: Inflammation may persist and fusion may recur after surgery.

recommendations.statement: For extragenital disease, UVA1 phototherapy is a potential first-line option; potent topical steroids and topical calcipotriol, possibly under occlusion, may also be tried.
recommendations.rationale: Fewer treatment studies are available for extragenital disease.

recommendations.statement: If treatment is needed during pregnancy or breastfeeding, limited amounts of potent topical steroids may be used; topical calcineurin inhibitors are contraindicated.
Do not use retinoids during pregnancy or for at least 2 years before conception, and use them cautiously in females of child-bearing age.

Refer inadequately responsive active disease to a physician specializing in the condition; arrange assessment and follow-up by an experienced specialist if differentiated or undifferentiated VIN or SCC develops in the setting of LS.

Review after 3 months to assess treatment response and review stable disease annually; a GP may conduct annual review of well-controlled disease if this arrangement is communicated to both patient and GP.
Advise prompt medical review for a new lump or sore area, changes in symptoms, or altered appearance.
For a diagnosis of vulval erosive LP, the proposed criteria suggest that at least three of the listed clinical or histological criteria should be present.

Biopsy when the clinical diagnosis is uncertain or coexisting intraepithelial neoplasia or SCC is suspected; perform direct immunofluorescence if an immunobullous disorder is in the differential diagnosis.
recommendations.rationale: Clinico-pathological correlation matters because only 25% are classic on biopsy.

recommendations.statement: Investigate for autoimmune disease only when there is clinical suspicion; obtain a skin swab to exclude secondary infection, especially in excoriated lesions, and use patch testing when medicament contact allergy is suspected.
A UK study concluded that routine viral hepatitis screening is unnecessary; screening may nevertheless be prudent in populations with a high prevalence of viral hepatitis.
recommendations.rationale: A cited UK study of 100 women with vulval mucosal LP did not find increased incidence.

recommendations.statement: Provide written information about the condition and its small long-term risk of neoplastic change; advise urgent medical assessment for a new lump, skin hardening or persistent ulceration.
Use an ultrapotent topical steroid, for example clobetasol proprionate, for vulval erosive disease.
recommendations.context: Recommended topical regimen; the optimal regimen has not been established.

recommendations.statement: Provide maintenance treatment when needed, either with a weaker steroid preparation or with less frequent application of a potent steroid.

For vaginal involvement, corticosteroid ointment applied to a tampon overnight may help; hydrocortisone rectal foam introduced vaginally with an applicator 1–2 times daily may be useful, while prednisolone suppositories may be used for more severe disease.
recommendations.rationale: Delivering corticosteroids to the vagina is difficult.

recommendations.statement: Topical pimecrolimus or tacrolimus may be used as alternative treatments; pimecrolimus may be better tolerated.
Mycophenolate mofetil and cyclosporin may be considered for selected cases.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence for systemic agents is limited and there is no consensus on their use.

recommendations.statement: For severe flares, oral steroids such as prednisolone 40 mg/day may be given and tapered over a few weeks; courses may be repeated when necessary.
Acitretin may help hypertrophic disease, but is contraindicated during pregnancy; avoid pregnancy for 2 years after treatment and use caution in other females of child-bearing age.
recommendations.rationale: Acitretin is severely teratogenic.

recommendations.statement: Reserve TNF-a inhibitors for the most recalcitrant cases.
recommendations.rationale: These agents have been reported to induce LP-like eruptions, including erosive oral and vulval disease.

recommendations.statement: Monitor potentially toxic systemic therapies carefully, preferably under dermatologist supervision in a specialized clinic.

Surgery may be needed for symptomatic vulval or vaginal adhesions and scarring, but do not operate while inflammatory disease is active; routinely use potent topical steroids immediately after surgical adhesiolysis for vulvo–vaginal LP.
recommendations.rationale: Postoperative potent topical steroids have been shown to improve longer-term function and outcomes.

recommendations.statement: Topical steroids may be used during pregnancy or breastfeeding; topical calcineurin inhibitors are not licensed in these periods, and retinoids are contraindicated during pregnancy and for at least 2 years before conception.
Refer erosive disease, recalcitrant cases, or patients being considered for systemic treatment to a multidisciplinary vulval clinic.
Review treatment response at 2–3 months, assess active disease as clinically needed, and provide long-term specialist follow-up for erosive vulval disease.
Review stable disease annually except in well-counselled patients who control their symptoms well; if the GP will conduct review, communicate this to both patient and GP.
Advise urgent medical assessment if a lump, skin hardening or persistent ulceration develops.

Explain the diagnosis verbally and in writing, acknowledge that the pain is real and may substantially affect quality of life, and discuss current understanding of contributing factors, treatment and prognosis.
Use a multidimensional approach to care.
recommendations.rationale: This approach is widely recommended, although the evidence levels are low.

recommendations.statement: Advise avoidance of irritants and use of emulsifying ointments and soap substitutes.

For introital dyspareunia due to provoked vestibulodynia, a local anaesthetic such as 5% lidocaine ointment or 2% lidocaine gel may be prescribed; apply lidocaine 10–20 min before penetrative sex and wash it off immediately before penetration.
recommendations.context: Topical pain modifiers; long-term daily Lidocaine 5% used four times a day for 12 weeks was not more effective than placebo for vestibular pain.

recommendations.statement: Current evidence is insufficient to recommend cannabis for vulvodynia.
recommendations.rationale: The guide states that evidence is insufficient to recommend it for this condition.

recommendations.statement: Integrate Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve stimulation (TENS), which patients can administer themselves, into a multidimensional strategy when used.
Offer physical therapy as a first-line treatment, preferably with a physiotherapist experienced in chronic vulvar pain and its sexual effects.
recommendations.context: Therapy may include education, pelvic floor exercises with biofeedback, manual therapy and dilation, alone or in combination.
recommendations.rationale: Treatment targets pelvic floor function and desensitization of painful tissue.

recommendations.statement: Offer psychosexual interventions, which may include cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT), pain management, sex therapy or psychoeducation, individually or in combination.
recommendations.rationale: These interventions address pain alongside sexual functioning, well-being and relationship satisfaction.

recommendations.statement: Lifestyle advice could form part of multidimensional care.
recommendations.context: The document notes a lack of evidence specific to women with vulvodynia for the cited lifestyle associations and benefits.

recommendations.statement: Do not usually recommend surgery for pain attributed to dysfunctional pain processing; consider vestibulectomy only as a last resort for provoked vestibulodynia after all available therapeutic options have failed.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence supporting vestibulectomy is of low quality.

recommendations.statement: Provide long-term multidisciplinary follow-up, with visits every 3 months until improvement.
Biopsy all lesions to map disease.
recommendations.rationale: Disease may be multifocal.

recommendations.statement: Immunohistochemistry for p16 and p53 can help distinguish HSIL from dVIN.
recommendations.rationale: The document describes HSIL as p16 positive with normal p53, and dVIN as p16 negative with p53 mutations.

recommendations.statement: For HSIL, imiquimod cream is a newer treatment option; other listed approaches are surgical cold knife excision, Laser CO2 therapy, Loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP), and follow-up without treatment in view of possible spontaneous regression.
recommendations.context: HSIL management; the document identifies imiquimod cream as a newer treatment modality.
recommendations.rationale: Surgical treatment has been the first choice, but recurrence is common and quality of life and sexual function may be adversely affected.

recommendations.statement: Treat DVIN with surgical cold knife excision.
Maintain close follow-up throughout life; for HSIL, review every 6–12 months and perform an annual cervical smear.
For DVIN, tailor lifelong follow-up to the underlying disease, with review at least every 6 months.

document_sections.heading: Changes to this guideline since the 2015 version:
document_sections.content: The update adds a scale for assessing genital psoriasis lesions, discusses ixekizumab, secukinumab and ustekinumab for genital psoriasis, introduces diagnostic criteria for vulval lichen planus, and changes first-line management advice for vulvodynia.

document_sections.heading: Search strategy
document_sections.content: The authors reviewed British Association for Sexual Health and HIV guidelines and searched MEDLINE, MEDLINE process, Embase and the Cochrane library through June 2021 without a starting-date restriction. Title and abstract searches covered Vulval lichen sclerosus, Vulval lichen planus, Vulval eczema, Vulval lichen simplex, Vulval psoriasis, Vulval intraepithelial neoplasia, High-grade SIL of the vulva, vulval HSIL, and Vulval pain syndromes/vulvodynia.

document_sections.heading: Scope
document_sections.content: The guideline addresses Vulval dermatitis (eczema), Psoriasis, Lichen simplex chronicus, Lichen sclerosus, Lichen planus, Vulvodynia and Vulval intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN).

document_sections.heading: General advice for delivery of vulval care
document_sections.content: Dermatologists, genitourinary medicine physicians, gynaecologists and primary care physicians may encounter vulval conditions. Because assessment and treatment cross these specialties, care is best coordinated through multidisciplinary management, explicit referral routes or a specialist multidisciplinary vulval service. Clinico-pathological services should be available for discussion and review of histology.

document_sections.heading: Physical examination of the patient
document_sections.content: Obtain informed consent before examination, investigation or treatment, with particular care for intimate anogenital examinations. Offer a chaperone every time and record that offer. Explain the examination before the patient undresses; protect privacy and dignity during dressing, undressing and examination. Ensure that the necessary facilities and equipment are ready and that the room is private, soundproofed and well lit, with an adjustable examination couch. Dermatoses and STIs can coexist; consider STI screening according to symptoms and risk factors in every patient. With vulval itch, particularly increased discharge, exclude vulvovaginal candidiasis. If anti-candidal treatment does not relieve symptoms, especially when candida cultures are negative, undertake a complete genital examination including speculum examination unless recently performed, and consider lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, lichen simplex chronicus, psoriasis and neoplasia, particularly HPV-related vulval intra-epithelial neoplasia in young women. Consider sexual dysfunction as either a cause or a consequence of symptoms and assess it when appropriate. Genital ulcers warrant consideration of STI testing even when an ulcerating dermatosis is present; herpes simplex and syphilis testing is recommended. Investigate concurrent STIs when lesions do not heal with standard treatment. Skin disease can be an early manifestation of HIV-related immunosuppression, and associated conditions may be more severe. Possible manifestations include numerous hyperkeratotic warts, treatment-resistant seborrheic dermatitis and new or severe psoriasis. Consider HIV testing in all patients, particularly with these findings.

document_sections.heading: General advice for all vulval conditions
document_sections.content: Avoid soap, shampoo and bubble bath on the affected area; simple emollients can serve as soap substitutes and moisturizers. Avoid irritating tight clothing and condoms lubricated with spermicide or containing local anaesthetics. Explain the diagnosis and long-term implications thoroughly, reinforce the explanation with accurate written information, and seek consent before informing the patient's GP about diagnosis and management.

document_sections.heading: Topical treatments
document_sections.content: Prefer ointments on anogenital skin: they need fewer preservatives and therefore present less risk of secondary contact allergy, whereas the higher water content of creams can cause stinging. Regular barrier-emollient application may shield affected skin from urine, menstrual blood and other local irritants.

document_sections.heading: Sexual partners
document_sections.content: Partner tracing is unnecessary unless STI screening identifies an infection.

document_sections.heading: Vulval dermatitis (Eczema)
document_sections.content: Dermatitis, also called eczema, is an inflammatory reaction with histological spongiosis, variable acanthosis and a superficial dermal lymphohistiocytic infiltrate. Itch is the principal symptom; both endogenous and exogenous factors may contribute. Do not label every itchy erythematous vulval condition as eczema: use the more specific diagnosis, such as atopic dermatitis or irritant/allergic contact dermatitis.

document_sections.heading: Aetiology
document_sections.content: For Vulval dermatitis (Eczema), increasing evidence implicates defective skin-barrier function in atopic dermatitis. The genital area is spared in many atopic people, although vulval lichen simplex chronicus can represent atopic dermatitis alone or alongside disease elsewhere. Irritant contact dermatitis is the commonest vulval eczema: vulval epithelium provides a less effective barrier than skin elsewhere and is exposed to moisture and friction. Cleansers, fragrances, lubricants and other topical products can aggravate it, especially with urinary incontinence. Allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV delayed hypersensitivity response to an applied product; common allergens include fragrances, antibiotics, local anaesthetics and ingredients of topical treatments. Seborrhoeic dermatitis is an inflammatory, scaling condition primarily affecting scalp and face and less often trunk. It may coexist with psoriasis and resemble it histologically; cutaneous yeast may contribute in predisposed people. Its redness is less sharply outlined than that of psoriasis.

document_sections.heading: Symptoms
document_sections.content: Vulval dermatitis (Eczema) may cause pruritus, soreness and pain.

document_sections.heading: Signs
document_sections.content: Vulval dermatitis (Eczema) commonly produces symmetrical erythema of the labia majora and minora, sometimes extending to perianal skin and the gluteal cleft; allergic contact dermatitis may extend to the thighs. Other findings include excoriations, acute erosions, serous oozing with crusting especially when secondarily infected, keratin accumulation between the labia, and lichenification in chronic disease.

document_sections.heading: Complications
document_sections.content: Vulval dermatitis (Eczema) can lead to secondary infection or lichen simplex chronicus.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Vulval dermatitis (Eczema) is generally diagnosed from history and examination; examine other skin for atopic or seborrhoeic changes. Distinguish psoriasis by its usually well-defined plaques and more frequent fissures, aided by examination of scalp, nails and other skin. Candidiasis can produce symmetrical, poorly defined erythema even without vaginal symptoms; a vulval swab helps assess it. Consider tinea cruris, although uncommon in women, for sharply bounded annular or circinate erythema with a scaly periphery and papular or pustular edge. Streptococcus A can cause symmetrical erythema as a primary infection or superinfection.

document_sections.heading: Investigation
document_sections.content: For Vulval dermatitis (Eczema), biopsy is seldom needed but should be performed for atypical features or failure to respond (GRADE 1,D). Use patch testing when allergic contact dermatitis is suspected, not routinely for every dermatitis type, and have a clinic experienced in testing and interpretation perform it (GRADE 1,B). Alongside the standard baseline allergen series, test suspected vulval allergic contact dermatitis against medicaments, preservatives and the patient's vulval products at suitable dilutions. Interpret relevance carefully: a positive test does not establish that the product caused the rash, and a negative test cannot fully exclude it. Suitable swabs help exclude candidiasis and bacterial infection; skin scrapings help rule out tinea cruris.

document_sections.heading: Management
document_sections.content: For Vulval dermatitis (Eczema), avoid suspected irritants and allergens, including cleansers, fragrances and wet wipes. Address urinary incontinence; uro-gynaecology referral can help. Use a bland emollient such as emulsifying ointment in place of soap, and consider barrier products particularly with substantial incontinence. Mild disease may be treated with 1% hydrocortisone ointment; more severe disease may require mometasone furoate or betamethasone valerate 0.025%. Apply the topical steroid once daily for 7–10 days until signs and symptoms settle, then as needed for recurrence. Treat concurrent infection with a steroid/antifungal or steroid/antibacterial combination. Antihistamines may relieve disturbed sleep.

document_sections.heading: Unlicensed treatments
document_sections.content: For resistant Vulval dermatitis (Eczema), topical tacrolimus or pimecrolimus may be tried without a licence for this indication. Application-site stinging limits use but may diminish with continued treatment.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up
document_sections.content: Vulval dermatitis (Eczema) does not routinely require follow-up. Review patients needing a stronger topical steroid or having difficulty controlling symptoms.

document_sections.heading: Patient information
document_sections.content: Explain Vulval dermatitis (Eczema), including its potential to recur. Discuss hygiene practices that can worsen it and provide relevant patient-information websites.

document_sections.heading: Vulval psoriasis
document_sections.content: This section addresses genital manifestations of psoriasis, including localized disease, wider involvement and less common pustular or erythrodermic presentations.

document_sections.heading: Aetiology
document_sections.content: Psoriasis is immune-mediated and genetically predisposed. Genital lesions affect up to 63% of patients during their lifetime; adult psoriasis prevalence ranges from 0.5 to 11.4%, and isolated genital lesions occur in 2–5%. Described triggers include infections such as streptococcal infection or HIV, smoking, excessive alcohol, physical factors such as tattoos, piercing or trauma, and medicines including systemic steroids, beta-blockers, lithium, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and antimalarials drugs. Recent studies find evidence for stress as a trigger inconclusive. Risk factors for vulval involvement include onset after 20 years of age, scalp or nail lesions, inverse psoriasis and higher Psoriasis Activity Score Index (PASI). Vulval psoriasis may accompany localized or disseminated psoriasis vulgaris, including extensor or gluteal-cleft lesions, and occasionally inverse psoriasis involving folds and genitalia. Rare generalized pustular psoriasis may spread from the genital region. Impetigo herpetiformis is a rare pregnancy-associated eruption beginning in intertriginous areas, including the vulva, typically in the last trimester and resolving rapidly postpartum; clinically and histologically it corresponds to pustular psoriasis. Uncommon erythrodermic psoriasis may affect more than 90% of body surface, including the vulva.

document_sections.heading: Symptoms
document_sections.content: For Vulval psoriasis, pruritus is reported most often; pain, burning and dyspareunia may also occur.

document_sections.heading: Evaluation
document_sections.content: The Genital Psoriasis Symptoms Scale (GPSS) captures patients' ratings of pruritus, pain, discomfort, stinging, burning, redness, scaling and cracking on a 11-point scale. The Static Physicians’ Global Assessment of Genitalia (sPGA-G) evaluates erythema, induration and scaling on a 6-point scale.

document_sections.heading: Associated disorders
document_sections.content: Psoriatic arthritis occurs in 15–30% of people with psoriasis vulgaris or exudative psoriasis; joint severity does not correlate with genital lesions. Cardiovascular disease, hypertension, malignancy, diabetes, metabolic syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease and autoimmune disease can accompany psoriasis. In patients with HIV, psoriasis may be more frequent, atypical and resistant to treatment.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Vulval psoriasis is usually diagnosed clinically from history and examination. Inspect common extragenital sites, including scalp, nails, natal cleft and umbilicus.

document_sections.heading: Investigation
document_sections.content: Dermoscopy may show dotted vessels or tortuous capillaries in psoriatic lesions. Characteristic histology includes parakeratosis, Munro micro-abscesses containing stratum-corneum neutrophils, absence of the granular layer, epidermal hyperplasia, frequent basal-layer mitoses and dilated tortuous capillaries in dermal papillae. Consider assessment for associated inflammatory conditions.

document_sections.heading: Signs
document_sections.content: Vulval psoriasis presents as symmetrical, uniform, well-defined erythematous plaques with rounded edges. Fine silvery scale is possible but less common on genital skin; outer labia majora may have thicker scale than inner surfaces or labia minora. Plaques can reach inguinal, perineal or pubic skin, and painful fissures may occur. Rare generalized pustular disease may begin as pustules on erythematous macules spreading from vulva and flexural folds across the body.

document_sections.heading: Management
document_sections.content: For Vulval psoriasis, avoid recognized triggers, including scented detergents, synthetic underwear and tight trousers. Localized disease calls for topical treatment; systemic treatment for disseminated or generalized psoriasis also treats genital lesions. Avoid anthralin, tazarotene and ultraviolet therapy on the vulva because of possible local adverse reactions, chiefly irritation.

document_sections.heading: Recommended regimens
document_sections.content: Topical treatment aims to thin plaques, reduce erythema and remove scale. Present available choices to agree on an acceptable individualized regimen. Solutions, foams or gels can be preferable on hair-bearing pubic skin; 0.5 fingertip unit should cover the genital area. Sequential or rotating topical corticosteroids, using mid potency followed by low potency preparations, are recommended (GRADE 1, B); frequency and duration depend on the selected steroid and response. Topical vitamin D analogues are recommended alone or with topical corticosteroids (GRADE 1, B). Coal tar, for example 1–5% liquor carbonis detergens in aqueous cream, is suggested alone or with topical corticosteroids (GRADE 2, C). Emollients are recommended to limit irritation from other topical therapies and sustain treatment gains (GRADE 1, B). A 2020 double-blinded, randomized, vehicle-controlled study found promising genital-psoriasis results with crisaborole. Dapsone combined with topical treatment was reported effective for vulval pustular psoriasis at 100 mg/day for 1 month.

document_sections.heading: Pregnancy and Breast-feeding
document_sections.content: For Vulval psoriasis, emollients are regarded as safe during pregnancy and lactation. Pregnancy and breastfeeding were exclusion criteria in the cited topical corticosteroid and vitamin D analogue studies, and information on excretion into breast milk is unavailable. Topical calcineurin inhibitors are not licensed during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Brief topical coal tar use in pregnancy is considered to carry only a small risk. Avoid ustekinumab, secukinumab, ixekizumab and guselkumab during pregnancy; decide on their use while breastfeeding by weighing risks and benefits for mother and child.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up
document_sections.content: Assess active Vulval psoriasis when clinically necessary and review stable disease after 1–3 months.

document_sections.heading: Systemic treatment
document_sections.content: Systemic methotrexate, retinoids, cyclosporine or biological agents may be used for disseminated or generalized psoriasis involving the genitals or genital psoriasis refractory to topical regimens (GRADE 1, A). Depending on national prescribing protocols, biologics may be authorized for isolated genital disease with substantial functional and quality-of-life effects. A randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in 2018 reported improvement in genital erosions, ulcers, fissures, pruritus and sexual life with ixekizumab, described as an anti-IL 17A monoclonal antibody. An open label randomized controlled study in 2021 found comparable efficacy and safety for secukinumab, another anti-IL 17A monoclonal antibody. Ustekinumab, an anti-IL 12/23 monoclonal antibody, has shown effectiveness. An observational study reported good genital and facial psoriasis outcomes and assessed quality-of-life effects with guselkumab.

document_sections.heading: Unlicensed treatments
document_sections.content: Topical tacrolimus and pimecrolimus have been reported effective without a licence for Vulval psoriasis (GRADE 2, C). Reported adverse events include contact dermatitis and local mycotic or viral infections.

document_sections.heading: Lichen simplex chronicus
document_sections.content: Anogenital lichen simplex chronicus is common, although incidence and prevalence are not firmly established. Estimated occurrence is approximately 0.5% in Western European and American populations, and it may account for 10–35% of vulval-clinic patients. Onset is usually in mid- to late-adulthood.

document_sections.heading: Aetiology
document_sections.content: An atopic predisposition is frequent in anogenital lichen simplex chronicus: up to 75% have personal or immediate-family atopy. Primary disease arises on otherwise normal vulval skin, usually in atopic people; secondary disease overlies itchy conditions such as eczema, psoriasis, lichen sclerosus or fungal or yeast infection. Psychological distress, including anxiety, depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder, and heat, sweat, dry skin, friction or harsh skincare may trigger it. Uraemia, liver disease and thyroid disease can predispose through generalized itch. Neuropathic itch is probably uncommon but can merit consideration, including with sacral spinal compression, postherpetic neuralgia or diabetic neuropathy. Epidermal hyperinnervation appears important in persistent itch.

document_sections.heading: Symptoms
document_sections.content: Lichen simplex chronicus causes severe chronic or intermittent itch, often in the evening or during sleep. Erosions or ulcers may produce burning, soreness and dyspareunia.

document_sections.heading: Signs
document_sections.content: Findings include ill-defined lichenified plaques that may be more pronounced opposite the dominant hand and feel leathery; erosions, ulcers or fissures; increased, decreased or absent pigmentation; and broken hairs where scratching or rubbing occurs.

document_sections.heading: Complications
document_sections.content: Lichen simplex chronicus may cause secondary infection. Deep, persistent scratching can produce severe irreversible architectural damage. Vulval lichen simplex chronicus does not appear to increase squamous cell cancer risk.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Ask about atopy in the patient or first-degree relatives and about diagnosed or undiagnosed skin disease elsewhere. Examination is usually sufficient for Lichen simplex chronicus; findings elsewhere can clarify the differential diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: Investigation
document_sections.content: For Lichen simplex chronicus, reserve biopsy for diagnostic uncertainty; histology may not readily distinguish it from psoriasis. Screen for infection when indicated, including Staphylococcus aureus or Candida albicans. Refer for dermatological patch testing if contact allergy is suspected. Measure serum ferritin when low iron stores are suspected, for example in vegetarians, regular blood donors or women with menorrhagia.

document_sections.heading: Recommended regimens
document_sections.content: For Lichen simplex chronicus, improve the skin barrier with saline soaks followed, then replaced, by an unperfumed cream lubricant; petroleum-based lubricants are considered too greasy and are not recommended. Identify underlying disease. Severe disease may be treated with clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment once or twice daily, tapered slowly after improvement. For milder disease, prescribe fluticasone propionate 0.005% or mometasone furoate 0.1% ointment once or twice daily, tapering promptly once improvement starts. Very thick plaques may receive intralesional triamcinolone. Intermittent ice may help, but limit each application to a maximum of 15 min to avoid cold injury. For nocturnal scratching, consider a sedating antihistamine such as hydroxyzine or a tricyclic antidepressant such as amitriptyline.

document_sections.heading: Alternative regimens
document_sections.content: For Lichen simplex chronicus, unlicensed second-line pimecrolimus 1% cream or tacrolimus 0.1% ointment may be used twice daily for up to 12 weeks. Other reported approaches are narrow band ultraviolet B administered with a comb-like device, Excimer 308-nm laser, high-intensity focused ultrasound and silk underwear. The proposed explanation for the laser effect is less cellular DNA damage and reduced epidermal hyperinnervation. Silk underwear may reduce topical-steroid requirements.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up
document_sections.content: Review mild Lichen simplex chronicus as clinically needed. For severe disease requiring potent topical corticosteroids, review at 4 weeks and thereafter as needed.

document_sections.heading: Lichen sclerosus
document_sections.content: Lichen sclerosus (LS) is an inflammatory disorder that affects anogenital skin more often than other skin, typically spares the vagina and very rarely affects oral mucosa. It mainly affects adult women but can occur in children. It is probably underdiagnosed; one study estimated incidence in women by age 80 at 1.6%. Female disease is usually chronic. Early diagnosis and treatment prevent scarring and may prevent malignancy; treat asymptomatic LS to prevent scarring. Spontaneous remission can occur.

document_sections.heading: Aetiology
document_sections.content: The cause of LS remains unknown, although genetic susceptibility is implicated. Approximately 10% of patients with vulval LS report affected family members, possibly an underestimate. Increased autoantibodies against extracellular matrix protein 1 and BP180 antigen have been reported; their meaning is uncertain but could support a humoral autoimmune contribution. Oxidative DNA injury found throughout LS biopsies suggests that oxidative damage to lipids, DNA and proteins may contribute to sclerosis, autoimmunity and cancer. A possible role for TP53 mutations in LS-related vulval cancer has been proposed. Potential triggers include mechanical irritation from tight clothing or bicycle saddles, with Koebnerization, and urine exposure or incontinence.

document_sections.heading: Symptoms
document_sections.content: LS may produce itch, particularly in female genital disease, soreness, dyspareunia or apareunia, painful or weak urinary flow, and constipation or other symptoms when perianal skin is involved, especially in children. It can also be asymptomatic.

document_sections.heading: Signs
document_sections.content: LS may show pale white hypertrophic or atrophic areas on vulval, perianal or extragenital skin; hyperkeratosis, sclerosis, mild erythema, frequent genital purpura, anogenital fissures and erosions. Blisters are very rare. Changes may remain vulval or form a ‘figure-ofeight’ distribution involving perianal skin. Scarring can resorb the labia minora and fuse tissue over the clitoris, burying it without destroying it. Extragenital disease may show follicular plugging.

document_sections.heading: Complications
document_sections.content: LS can affect self-esteem, including through concern about clitoral appearance, and cause clitoral pseudo-cysts, sexual or urinary dysfunction and dysaesthesia. The stated actual risk of ano-genital squamous cell carcinoma is <5%.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Recognize LS by its characteristic appearance. Typical disease may not require biopsy, although many clinicians obtain one initially. Biopsy is indicated for diagnostic uncertainty, suspected dysplasia or carcinoma, or failure of first-line treatment (GRADE 1, A). Correlate clinical and histopathological findings because early histology can lack specificity. Sample a representative lesion. Histological findings include hyperkeratosis, epidermal atrophy, basal hydropic degeneration with possible pigmentary incontinence, a lymphohistiocytic infiltrate in a hyaline upper-dermal band with loss of elastic tissue, and follicular plugging in hair-bearing skin.

document_sections.heading: Further investigations
document_sections.content: For LS, investigate associated autoimmune conditions when clinically indicated, including thyroid disease, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo and diabetes mellitus; these can lack symptoms. Use bacterial, fungal or viral swabs only when symptoms or signs suggest a concurrent infection. Patch testing is rarely needed, reserved for suspected secondary allergy to a medicament, with dermatological advice.

document_sections.heading: Management
document_sections.content: Explain LS and provide written information. Discuss its small neoplastic risk while noting that well-controlled LS may not confer increased risk. Advise prompt contact for a lump, ulcer, hardening, changed appearance or texture, or major symptom change. Recommend emollients and minimizing genital irritation from cleansers, frequent water exposure, incontinence or cloths; cycling or horse riding aggravates symptoms in some people. Emollients may ease symptoms following initial steroid treatment.

document_sections.heading: Specific treatment
document_sections.content: Ultra-potent or potent topical steroids, such as clobetasol proprionate or mometasone furoate, are recommended first line for genital LS (GRADE 1, A).

document_sections.heading: Recommended regimen
document_sections.content: LS regimens vary. A common approach applies a potent to ultra-potent topical steroid, usually once daily, for three months. Another applies it daily for one month, on alternate days for one month, then twice weekly for one month, reviewing at 3 months; this may be preferable in children to avoid atrophy. Resistant disease may occasionally benefit from twice-daily application.

document_sections.heading: Maintenance treatment
document_sections.content: Proactive mometasone furoate 0.1% ointment or clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment twice weekly effectively and safely maintains LS remission and may help prevent malignant change. Thirty grams of an ultra-potent steroid should last at least 3 months (GRADE 1, A).

document_sections.heading: Treatment of superinfection
document_sections.content: If secondary infection is a concern in LS, a potent or ultra-potent topical steroid combined with antibacterial and antifungal agents, such as gentamycin or fucidic acid and nystatin or azole antifungals, or another product addressing secondary infection, may be appropriate. Use it only briefly to clear infection.

document_sections.heading: Allergies to topical preparations
document_sections.content: Prolonged topical treatment for LS can lead to allergy to any constituent, including the steroid. Consider allergy testing if a previously effective treatment begins losing effect.

document_sections.heading: Alternative second line treatments
document_sections.content: Topical calcineurin inhibitors are not licensed for LS. A comparative randomized study supported topical tacrolimus 0.1% in vulval LS: clobetasol proprionate 0.05% acted faster, both treatments worked after 12 weeks of daily application, and significantly fewer women in the clobetasol proprionate group still had LS. Another genital and extragenital LS study reported efficacy after 16 to 24 weeks of topical tacrolimus 0.1%: 77% of evaluable patients responded, 43% had complete response at 24 weeks, and no malignancy or dysplasia was found during 18 months of follow-up. Topical tacrolimus 0.03% ointment appears effective for children, probably mainly girls, with anogenital LS; twice-weekly maintenance may reduce recurrence. In a comparison after 12 weeks, pimecrolimus 1% cream and clobetasol propionate 0.05% cream both eased vulval itch and burning or pain, while clobetasol better reduced inflammation. A separate pimecrolimus study reported complete remission in 42% after 6 months. Initial local irritation was the commonest adverse effect of tacrolimus and pimecrolimus and usually improved; long-term risks need study because topical immunosuppression might increase malignancy risk. Two small RCTs of limited quality provide some support for systemic retinoids such as aciretin. Consider them after failure of standard LS therapy only under a dermatologist experienced with these agents. They are severely teratogenic; avoid pregnancy for at least 2 years after finishing. Phototherapy helps some patients; UVA1 has the best supporting data among UV approaches and may be considered after topical-corticosteroid failure, but carcinoma development after PUVA and UVB is a particular concern at genital sites. A systematic review found no high-quality evidence supporting lasers for male or female LS, and long-term efficacy and adverse-effect data are lacking. Reserve surgery in vulval LS for coexisting VIN/SCC or fusion; female disease tends to recur around scars. Evidence for Adipose-Derived Stem Cells (ADSC) and/or Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) remains weak, so these treatments currently cannot be recommended for vulvar LS.

document_sections.heading: Clitoral LS
document_sections.content: LS may be limited to the clitoral hood but often affects other vulval sites. Normally the prepuce covers part of the glans, protects and lubricates it, and retracts easily. Clitoral LS may start with preputial swelling, followed by white plaques, fissures, fusion or scarring. Examine the clitoris and treat involvement as at other genital sites. Avoid suspected mechanical triggers such as tight clothing and massage topical products gently into the skin. Surgery for fusion is indicated only rarely, such as for severe effects on self-esteem, sexual function or urination. Recurrence remains possible because inflammation may persist; an experienced surgeon should operate only after counselling on the procedure, adverse effects and recurrence.

document_sections.heading: Extragenital LS
document_sections.content: Treatment evidence is more limited for extragenital LS. UVA1 phototherapy is a possible first-line option. Potent topical steroids or topical calcipotriol, possibly with occlusion, may be tried.

document_sections.heading: Pregnancy and breast-feeding
document_sections.content: LS generally follows a favourable course in pregnancy and does not itself preclude vaginal delivery. If treatment is necessary, limited quantities of potent topical steroids are safe during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Topical calcineurin inhibitors are contraindicated in both periods. Retinoids are absolutely contraindicated during pregnancy and for at least 2 years before conception and require caution in females of child-bearing age.

document_sections.heading: Onward referral criteria
document_sections.content: Refer inadequately responsive active LS to a clinician specializing in the condition. Patients developing differentiated or undifferentiated VIN or SCC against a background of LS require assessment and follow-up by an experienced specialist.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up
document_sections.content: For LS, check response after 3 months. Review stable disease annually; a GP may do so when disease is well controlled, provided the specialist communicates the arrangement to patient and GP. Instruct patients to seek prompt assessment for a lump, sore area, altered symptoms or changed appearance.

document_sections.heading: Lichen planus
document_sections.content: Research initiatives are under way to prioritize clinical questions and standardize trial outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Aetiology
document_sections.content: Lichen planus (LP) is inflammatory and can affect skin, hair, nails, genital or oral mucosa and, less often, lacrimal duct, oesophagus or external auditory meatus. Its precise pathogenesis is unknown; a T-cell response to unidentified antigens is suspected. Weak circulating basement membrane zone antibodies occurred in 61% of 56 biopsy-confirmed erosive vulval LP patients, but their meaning is unknown. LP may overlap or coexist with LS. In a tertiary-hospital dermatology-clinic review, vulval LP accounted for 8.8% of patients.

document_sections.heading: Symptoms
document_sections.content: LP may cause itch or irritation, soreness, dyspareunia, urinary symptoms or vaginal discharge; some patients have no symptoms.

document_sections.heading: Signs
document_sections.content: Three principal anogenital LP patterns are described. Classical LP produces papules on keratinized anogenital skin, possibly with Wickham’s striae on the inner vulva; hyperpigmentation often remains after resolution, especially in dark skin, and symptoms may be absent. One study found vulval lesions in 19 out of 37 women with cutaneous LP, including four of the 19 without symptoms. Hypertrophic LP is relatively uncommon, hard to diagnose and chiefly perineal or perianal; thick warty plaques may ulcerate, become infected or painful, and resemble cancer, while vaginal lesions are usually absent. Erosive LP most often produces vulval symptoms: in 114 affected women, mean onset age for vulval symptoms was 56.9 years. Mucosa develops erosions with red-to-purple edges and sometimes surrounding pale Wickham’s striae. Vaginal disease can occur alone and requires early recognition and treatment to avert scarring or complete stenosis. Friable telangiectasias and patchy erythema can cause dyspareunia, postcoital bleeding and often serosanguinous variable discharge. Healing may create synechiae and scars. Oral erosive lesions occur too, although oral synechiae are uncommon; concurrent vulval, vaginal and gingival erosions are termed vulvo–vaginal–gingival syndrome and usually cause pain and soreness.

document_sections.heading: Diagnostic criteria
document_sections.content: An international e-Delphi exercise proposed diagnosing vulval erosive LP when at least three criteria occur: clearly bounded erosions or erythema at the vaginal entrance; a hyperkeratotic lesion edge and/or adjacent Wickham striae; pain or burning; scarring or architectural loss; vaginal inflammation; another affected mucosal surface; a defined inflammatory band at the dermo-epidermal junction; an inflammatory band composed mainly of lymphocytes; and basal-layer degeneration. In a study of 243 women with clinically suspected vulval LP and available histology, alongside 50 biopsy-confirmed vulvar LS patients and 50 with culture-confirmed chronic vulvovaginal candidiasis, erosions, glazed erythema, oral involvement, pain or burning and a hyperkeratotic margin significantly distinguished conditions. A score ≥2 correlated with histological vulvar LP with 100% sensitivity and specificity of 92% against vulvar LS and 88% against chronic vulvovaginal candidiasis. Vaginal disease practically excludes lichen sclerosus, which usually spares non-keratinized mucosa, although LP and LS can overlap elsewhere. Cicatricial mucous membrane pemphigoid and pemphigus may resemble erosive LP. Potentially helpful dermoscopic findings are diffusely distributed thick irregular linear vessels, peripheral Wickham’s striae and intense background redness. Classical vulval LP histology includes irregular saw-tooth acanthosis, a thickened granular layer, basal-cell liquefaction and a band-shaped, predominantly lymphocytic dermal infiltrate, although biopsy may be nonspecific. Erosive mucosal LP may show marked epithelial apoptosis, lymphocytic inflammation, plasma cells and ulceration with more typical LP findings at ulcer edges; vulval erosive LP also shows widespread disruption of basement membrane zone structures, including hemidesmosomes and anchoring fibrils. Keratinized-skin vulvar LP varies substantially: basal-layer degeneration best distinguishes it from nodular prurigo and lichenified psoriasis, but superinfection-related inflammation can conceal or mimic it. Pseudo-epitheliomatous hyperplasia may resemble microinvasive SCC, while granulomatous infiltrates can resemble systemic autoimmune or infectious disease.

document_sections.heading: Further investigations
document_sections.content: For LP, biopsy if clinical diagnosis is uncertain or accompanying intraepithelial neoplasia or SCC is suspected. Perform direct immunofluorescence when considering an immunobullous disorder. Only 25% have classic biopsy findings, so clinical–pathological correlation matters. Investigate thyroid or other autoimmune disease only on clinical suspicion because association with vulval LP is rare. Swab excoriated lesions, particularly to exclude secondary infection; patch-test when medicament contact allergy is suspected. Although associations with hepatitis C and sometimes B have been observed in some countries, particularly Mediterranean countries, a UK study of 100 women with vulval mucosal LP found no increased incidence and judged routine screening unnecessary. Screening may nevertheless be prudent in populations with high viral-hepatitis prevalence.

document_sections.heading: Complications
document_sections.content: Erosive LP particularly can scar and cause vaginal synechiae. In the only reported prospective study, among 114 vulvar LP patients followed for a mean of six years, seven developed vulval intraepithelial neoplasia and two (1.8%) developed anogenital SCC. Reports describe frequent inguinal metastasis, recurrent vulval cancer in diseased mucosa and disease-related death in LP-associated SCC. Conversely, a clinicohistopathological review of 43 consecutive vulvectomies or wide local excisions for HPV-independent vulvar SCC across an 11year period found no LP; all cases were judged to have underlying LS. Those authors considered LP-associated vulvar SCC rare and cautioned that differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia can superficially mimic erosive or hypertrophic LP. Whether early treatment, effective control or prolonged maintenance reduces malignancy risk remains unknown.

document_sections.heading: Management
document_sections.content: Vulval LP, particularly erosive disease, may substantially impair quality of life and sexual function. Explain the condition and provide written information. Discuss the small long-term neoplastic risk and advise urgent assessment for a lump, persistent ulcer, hardening or other change in appearance or texture.

document_sections.heading: Treatment
document_sections.content: Two randomized controlled trials provide evidence relevant to treating vulval erosive LP.

document_sections.heading: Topical treatment. Recommended Regimen
document_sections.content: Ultrapotent topical steroids such as clobetasol proprionate are recommended for vulval erosive LP (GRADE 2, B). In a vulval-clinic study of 114 patients, 89 received these steroids first line; 75% improved, 54% became symptom-free, and inflammatory signs resolved in only 9%. The optimal regimen lacks evidence. Maintenance may require a weaker steroid or less frequent potent-steroid application. Vaginal corticosteroid delivery is difficult; possibilities include overnight ointment on a tampon, hydrocortisone rectal foam inserted vaginally with an applicator 1–2 times daily, or prednisolone suppositories for more severe cases.

document_sections.heading: Alternative Regimens
document_sections.content: Topical pimecrolimus or tacrolimus may help vulval LP, with pimecrolimus possibly better tolerated. In a retrospective series of 16 women, topical tacrolimus controlled symptoms and improved lesions in all but one; benefit may be temporary and require ongoing use, which appeared safe and effective for disease control.

document_sections.heading: Systemic treatments
document_sections.content: Systemic LP treatment has little supporting evidence and no consensus. For vulvo–vaginal–gingival syndrome, azathioprine, dapsone, griseofulvin and minocycline, tried empirically, are generally considered of little or no benefit. Limited evidence most favours standard-dose hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate (MTX) and mycophenolate mofetil. A retrospective study reported response to hydroxychloroquine in 9 of 15 patients (60%), almost half with lasting benefit. Another study found significant improvement with long-term MTX in 19 of 27 erosive LP patients (70%), although other studies reported worse outcomes. Mycophenolate mofetil and cyclosporin may merit consideration in selected cases. For severe flares, oral prednisolone 40 mg/day can be tapered over a few weeks and courses repeated when needed. Acitretin may help hypertrophic LP but is severely teratogenic, absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy, and requires avoidance of pregnancy for 2 years after treatment and caution in other females of child-bearing age. A planned multicentre, four-arm, assessor-blind, randomized controlled trial comparing hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil and prednisolone added to standard topical treatment closed before reaching recruitment targets. Treatment success occurred only with hydroxychloroquine in 2/6 patients, 33%, and mycophenolate mofetil in 2/5 patients, 40%; methodological lessons may inform future studies. Biological agents have produced variable results. Because TNF-a inhibitors increasingly have been reported to provoke LP-like eruptions, including erosive oral and vulval disease, reserve them for the most recalcitrant cases. Basiliximab, an anti-IL-2 receptor antibody, was effective in one severe erosive oral LP case but has not been evaluated for vulval disease. These potentially toxic systemic treatments require careful monitoring, preferably by a dermatologist in a specialist clinic.

document_sections.heading: Surgery
document_sections.content: LP-related symptomatic vulval or vaginal adhesions and scarring may require surgery, but active inflammatory disease contraindicates it. In a study of 11 women with LP scarring, adhesiolysis enabled intercourse in 55%, improved urinary difficulty in 75%, and 91% were satisfied and would recommend surgery; sexual difficulties can nevertheless persist. Routinely use potent topical steroids immediately after vulvo–vaginal LP adhesiolysis to improve long-term outcomes and function. A prospective focused-ultrasound study reported positive responses in 127 of 135 patients with non-neoplastic vulval epithelial disorders, including all seven with vulval LP.

document_sections.heading: Pregnancy and Breast-feeding
document_sections.content: For LP, topical steroids are considered safe during pregnancy and breastfeeding; topical calcineurin inhibitors are not licensed in either period. Retinoids are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy and for at least 2 years before conception and should be used cautiously in other females of child-bearing age.

document_sections.heading: Onward referral
document_sections.content: Refer erosive LP, recalcitrant disease or cases being considered for systemic treatment to a multidisciplinary vulval clinic.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up
document_sections.content: For LP, assess treatment response after 2–3 months and reassess active disease as clinically required. Erosive vulval disease requires long-term specialist follow-up. Review stable disease annually except when well-counselled patients control their symptoms effectively. If the GP will review the patient, communicate this to both patient and GP. Advise urgent review of a lump, skin hardening, persistent ulcer or other change in appearance or texture.

document_sections.heading: Vulvodynia
document_sections.content: Vulvodynia denotes vulvar pain lasting at least 3 months without a clearly identifiable cause, potentially accompanied by associated factors. It is classified by generalized or localized distribution and provoked, unprovoked or mixed occurrence. Under the cited Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM5) version, it can be considered a female genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder.

document_sections.heading: Aetiology
document_sections.content: Vulvodynia is currently understood as dysfunctional sensory processing involving peripheral and central nervous systems. Comparable dysfunction occurs in fibromyalgia, interstitial cystitis/painful bladder, irritable bowel syndrome and temporomandibular joint dysfunction, all significantly associated with vulvodynia. Shared genetic predisposition is suspected. Pelvic-floor muscle dysfunction and psychosexual disturbances, whether pre-existing or resulting from chronic pain, are identified triggers or maintaining factors. Candidiasis and hormonal contraception are not established definitively as triggers. Women with vulvodynia report childhood sexual abuse and severe physical abuse more often than women without it.

document_sections.heading: Clinical features
document_sections.content: The section describes symptom onset, provocation, quality, location, severity and timing, alongside examination findings and psychological or sexual consequences.

document_sections.heading: Symptoms
document_sections.content: OPQRST can organize the account of vulvar discomfort. Onset often follows a physical event such as infection, dermatosis or pelvic surgery, or an emotional event; candidiasis as a trigger is disputed because infection is mostly self-reported. Provoked symptoms follow sexual penetration or touch, or nonsexual contact such as tampon insertion, tight clothing, sitting or gynaecological examination. Introital dyspareunia can be primary from first intercourse or secondary after previously painless intercourse. Unprovoked symptoms arise spontaneously without touch; mixed symptoms are spontaneous and aggravated by sexual or nonsexual contact. Burning predominates, but tingling, stinging, rawness, irritation and sometimes itch also occur. Generalized symptoms involve the entire vulva and may extend to thighs or perianal skin. Localized symptoms most often affect the vestibule, especially posteriorly, termed vestibulodynia; provoked vestibulodynia is the most reproducible subset. Labial pain and clitorodynia are less common locations. Severity varies markedly between patients and from day to day, with variable effects on intimacy, sexual communication, anxiety, depression, partner responses, catastrophizing and self-efficacy. Pain often precedes diagnosis by months or years; substantial improvement or full remission can occur spontaneously or after treatment.

document_sections.heading: Signs
document_sections.content: In Vulvodynia, vulval inspection is normal or reveals a lesion insufficient to explain the discomfort. Gentle vestibular pressure with a cotton-tipped applicator causes tenderness or pain in provoked vestibulodynia. Neurological examination is normal, without objective neurological findings.

document_sections.heading: Complications
document_sections.content: Vulvodynia can substantially affect psychological and sexual well-being and may require interventions addressing those effects.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Diagnose Vulvodynia clinically using history and examination after excluding other explanations for vulvar discomfort.

document_sections.heading: Differential diagnosis
document_sections.content: Consider neurological causes of perineal pain such as pudendal neuralgia with unilateral or diffuse vulvar pain accompanied by sphincter disturbance and objective neurological abnormalities. Pelvic or lumbosacral MRI can help exclude compression, while nerve blocks can aid diagnostic assessment.

document_sections.heading: Management
document_sections.content: Vulvodynia management combines explanation, vulval care and a multidimensional approach addressing pain, pelvic-floor function and psychosexual effects.

document_sections.heading: Information
document_sections.content: Provide both spoken and written explanation. Identify the condition as vulvodynia, affirm that pain is real and can greatly affect quality of life, and explain current knowledge of mechanisms, contributing factors, treatment and prognosis.

document_sections.heading: Multidimensional approach
document_sections.content: A multidimensional approach is widely recommended for vulvodynia, as for other chronic pain. Supporting evidence levels are low, and placebo responses are strong in vulvodynia and female sexual dysfunction.

document_sections.heading: Vulval care measures
document_sections.content: Avoid local irritants and use emulsifying ointments or soap substitutes.

document_sections.heading: Pain targeted treatments
document_sections.content: Topical pain modifiers are discussed under GRADE 2. For introital dyspareunia due to provoked vestibulodynia, 5% lidocaine ointment or 2% lidocaine gel is commonly prescribed 10–20 min before penetrative sex and washed away immediately before penetration. In a study, daily Lidocaine 5% applied four times a day for 12 weeks did not reduce vestibular pain more than placebo. Botulinum neurotoxin injected into bulbo-cavernosus muscles at 20–50 units was not better than placebo for pain. Efficacy of 2% amitryptiline cream, alone or with baclofen, requires further study. Benefit has not been demonstrated for 0.025% to 0.05% capsaicin cream, whose use is limited by burning. Although medical cannabis has been considered a possible chronic-pain or female-sexual-dysfunction treatment, evidence is insufficient to recommend it for vulvodynia. Oral pain modifiers are discussed under GRADE 2. Evidence does not adequately support the benefit of tricyclic antidepressants despite frequent use, especially for generalized unprovoked vulvodynia. Amitriptyline is used most often at 5 to 50 mg daily (IV); unlike uncontrolled studies, two small RCT studies of low or moderate quality did not establish efficacy, and tolerability is frequently poor. Desimipramine escalated from 25 mg to 150 mg for 12 weeks was no better than placebo. Oral milnacipran at 50–200 mg per day for 12 weeks reduced coital pain. Gabapentin at 1200 to 3000 mg per day did not outperform placebo for tampon-test pain or dyspareunia but improved sexual function, especially arousal. Evidence for pregabalin is limited. Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve stimulation (TENS) can be self-administered and fits best within multidimensional care. Efficacy remains unproven for fractional CO 2 laser therapy, low-level laser therapy and radiofrequency in vulvodynia; the FDA warns against energy devices for sexual-function, menopause or urinary-incontinence symptoms because of adverse-event concerns. Small trials found acupuncture, alone or with lidocaine, effective for pain and sexual functioning; work to improve study protocols and compare acupuncture strategies is ongoing.

document_sections.heading: Hormones
document_sections.content: Evidence and recommendations conflict on stopping combined hormonal contraception or adding topical oestrogen, alone or with testosterone.

document_sections.heading: Physical therapy
document_sections.content: Physical therapy is regarded as first-line Vulvodynia treatment (GRADE 1,B). It aims to restore pelvic-floor proprioception, relaxation, discrimination, elasticity and normal tone while desensitizing painful vulvar tissue. It combines education, ideally about anatomy and sexual function, with pelvic-floor exercises, biofeedback, manual treatment and dilation, separately or together. Physiotherapists experienced in chronic vulvar pain and sexual effects obtain the best results.

document_sections.heading: Psychosexual interventions
document_sections.content: Psychosexual interventions carry GRADE 1,B and can include cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT), pain management, sex therapy and psychoeducation, separately or combined. They address pain and the thoughts, emotions, behaviours and couple interactions affecting sexual function, well-being and relationship satisfaction. Studies found CBT improved intercourse pain as much as vestibulectomy and outperformed topical corticosteroids and supportive psychotherapy for pain reduction and sexual functioning. Couple-based CBT appears appropriate because both patient and partner can experience psychological and behavioural effects. Mindfulness is increasingly used with or instead of CBT. In cited comparisons, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) reduced intercourse pain more than CBT and produced similar other pain and sexual outcomes. Women with greater confidence in mindfulness, shorter relationships and secondary PVD might respond better to MBCT than CBT.

document_sections.heading: Lifestyle advice
document_sections.content: Inactivity, stress, poor sleep, unhealthy diet and smoking are associated with chronic-pain severity and persistence, and lifestyle change can benefit chronic pain. Although vulvodynia-specific evidence for these associations and benefits is absent, lifestyle advice could form part of multidimensional care.

document_sections.heading: Surgery
document_sections.content: Surgery is generally not recommended for chronic pain arising from dysfunctional pain processing, including vulvodynia. Despite low-quality evidence, posterior or total vestibulectomy, with or without vaginal advancement, is considered a last resort for provoked vestibulodynia only after all available treatments fail. Published studies report lasting reductions in introital dyspareunia and patient satisfaction. Improvement in sexual function is moderate or not superior to electromyographic biofeedback or CBT. Reported short- and long-term complications include bleeding, wound dehiscence, Bartholin’s cyst and an unsatisfactory cosmetic result. Table 1 compares successive terminology for vulval premalignant lesions; it does not describe a vulvodynia treatment.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up
document_sections.content: For Vulvodynia, provide multidisciplinary long-term follow-up (GRADE 1,B), with review every 3 months until improvement.

document_sections.heading: Health promotion
document_sections.content: Healthcare professionals need better education in Vulvodynia diagnosis and management. Diagnostic delay and inappropriate treatment may adversely affect prognosis.

document_sections.heading: Vulval intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN)
document_sections.content: This section addresses vulval squamous epithelial dysplasia and distinguishes the premalignant entities HSIL and DVIN.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: VIN is a chronic vulval skin disorder involving dysplastic squamous epithelial change. It is premalignant, although spontaneous regression has been described. Terminology has changed repeatedly since the first description in 1922. The International Society for the Study of Vulvovaginal Disease (ISSVD) approved its latest terminology in 2015: Low-grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (SIL) of the vulva or vulval LSIL; High-grade SIL of the vulva or vulval HSIL; and Vulval intraepithelial neoplasia, differentiated type. Table 1 traces how terminology across successive classifications maps to these categories.

document_sections.heading: Aetiology
document_sections.content: Under current ISSVD terminology, HSIL and DVIN are the two premalignant vulval lesions that can progress to vulval squamous cell carcinoma; they differ in cause, malignant potential and treatment. HSIL results from persistent high-risk Human Papilloma Virus (HPV) infection. Its incidence is approximately 5 per 100 000 women per year and is rising, with a peak at 35 to 49 years. More anogenital HPV infection and/or more liberal biopsy use may explain the increase. Smoking and immunocompromise are risk factors. DVIN is linked to LS and LP rather than HPV, occurs mainly in older women, represents less than 5% of VIN lesions, and has greater malignant potential than HSIL. Its cause is unclear.

document_sections.heading: Symptoms and signs
document_sections.content: The comparison of HSIL and DVIN shows that HSIL may cause itch, burning, irritation, pain or psychosexual complaints, or be asymptomatic; its variable lesions can be whitish, red or pigmented plaques and multifocal. DVIN symptoms often reflect underlying lichen sclerosus or lichen planus. DVIN may be hard to distinguish from lichen sclerosus, with a grey-white or red lesion, rough surface or ulceration; it is more often unifocal than HSIL.

document_sections.heading: Complications
document_sections.content: Both HSIL and DVIN can progress to vulval squamous cell carcinoma, recur frequently after treatment and produce psychosexual complaints.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosis
document_sections.content: HSIL and DVIN may be multifocal. Biopsy every lesion to map disease (GRADE 1).

document_sections.heading: Investigation
document_sections.content: HSIL biopsy can show disordered squamous epithelium, cytological atypia, increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and mitoses. DVIN histology is difficult to interpret and can show hyperplasia, hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, elongated interconnected rete ridges, basal-cell atypia, conspicuous nucleoli, atypical basal mitoses, dyskeratosis and rete-ridge hypermaturation. p16 and p53 immunohistochemistry can help distinguish them: HPV-driven HSIL is p16 positive with normal p53, whereas HPV-independent dVIN is p16 negative with p53 gene mutations. Two additional HPV-independent vulvar-cancer precursors are VAAD: Vulvar acanthosis with altered differentiation, and DEVIL: Differentiated exophytic vulvar intraepithelial lesion.

document_sections.heading: Management
document_sections.content: For HSIL, surgery has traditionally been preferred, but recurrence is frequent and quality of life and sexual function may suffer. Imiquimod cream is a newer immune-response-modifying option with indirect antiviral and antitumour properties (GRADE 1 B). Listed HSIL approaches are surgical cold knife excision, Laser CO2 therapy, Loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP), Imiquimod cream and observation without treatment in view of possible spontaneous regression. For DVIN, the listed treatment is surgical cold knife excision.

document_sections.heading: Follow up
document_sections.content: Lifelong close follow-up is mandatory. For HSIL, review every 6–12 months and perform an annual cervical smear. For DVIN, tailor review to underlying disease but assess at least every 6 months.

document_sections.heading: Vaccination
document_sections.content: Therapeutic HPV vaccines have produced varying clinical success but are not yet available for routine care. Prophylactic HPV vaccination began in 2007 to reduce cervical premalignant or malignant disease and other HPV-related lesions such as HSIL. Among women negative for HPV 16 or 18 before vaccination, quadrivalent HPV 6/11/16/18 and bivalent (16/18) vaccines prevent HPV 16- and 18-related high-grade vulval and vaginal lesions. The nonavalent vaccine covering HPV 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58 performs slightly better.
